2870.title: Token right after a digit, mostly a space
2870.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself, in a very local way: it fires on the token that comes immediately after a number, most often the blank space that follows a digit glued to a word or code (F1, Q1, Mk3, HTTP/1.1, MG42, and footnote or page numbers stuck to a word such as "imparted.2", "ratio1", "word41", "is61"). The preceding digit is usually a 1, 2 or 3, and what follows is often another number or the start of the next sentence. In the plot summaries the same thing shows up weakly on a suffix or word straight after a number ("2nd", "R2-D2", "1950's", "142 kilometers", "$750,000 loan"). It does not fire on the digit itself, nor on ordinary spaces between words where no number precedes.

2965.title: Word that directly follows a number or year
2965.explanation: The unit fires on the first ordinary word that comes straight after a number, above all after a four-digit year or season: "2014 Serbia", "2007 Bihar", "2013 Oklahoma", "2019-20 Milwaukee", "2021 Newfoundland", "1602 Shakespeare", "1862 Confederate", "2019 Georgian", and index or table entries such as "232 Shakespeare" and "1,027 Ships". It is strongest when that word is a capitalised place, nationality or person's name, and weaker for plain words after a number ("1950 painting", "1937 Los", "9000 computer", "$750,000 deal", "$18,000 into"). The same names without a number in front do not fire it, and neither do unit marks or symbols glued to a number (px, UTC, a closing bracket), which belong to the opposite pole.

2980.title: Unit or suffix right after a number ending in 1
2980.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token in its immediate spot: a short unit, letter or suffix glued directly onto a number whose last digit is 1. Examples are "m" after 1,421, 4,811, 171, 961, 111, €75.1 and £341 (metres or millions alike), "mm" after 11, "ha" after 0.41, "inch" after 1, "世纪" after 11, "n" in 802.11n, "X" in 1Xtra and 21X23, "B" in 221B, and "st" in 21st and 101st. The meaning of the unit is irrelevant; what matters is the digit 1 immediately before a non-digit suffix. It fires only weakly on the digit 1 itself or on a plain word after a number, and not when another digit follows the 1.

9325.title: Specific name fragments: -agu, -ili, Saras, -arti
9325.explanation: This layer-0 unit reacts to the marked token itself, not to meaning: it fires on a small fixed set of word pieces, most of them the middle or tail piece of a proper name. The strongest are 'agu' in Montagu (many times), 'ili' in Vasili, ' Saras' in Sarasu/Saraswati, 'arti' in Benzarti, 'arta' in Puerto Vallarta and 'anel' in Villanelle; weaker ones are ' arenas', ' getArguments', 'Marty', 'avenport' (Davenport), 'arcy' (Darcy) and 'appearances'. Many of the pieces contain the letters 'ar' or begin with 'a' plus a consonant, but there is no shared topic, and the surrounding text (book catalogues, Indian film plots, lists of fortifications, code) does not matter. Other names or other spellings of the same names do not fire it.

19352.title: Word piece "igrants" in "emigrants"
19352.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the word piece "igrants" that completes "em-igrants" (emigrants, Emigrants), whatever the setting, whether Cherokee removal, wagon trains, French royalist exiles, Cuban exiles or Wikipedia category lines such as "Indian emigrants to Canada". It is a spelling detector, not a meaning detector: the first, unsplit mention of "emigrants" in the same text does not carry the peak, and related words such as "emigrated", "emigrant", "migration" or "refugees" are not marked. Far weaker firings (under half strength) land on unrelated word pieces such as "oss" in Colossus, "izzard" in blizzard, "underneath", "ortho" and "ba", which share no idea with the main group.

51887.title: The word "district"
51887.explanation: The unit fires on the word "district" itself, capitalised or not, and on its pieces and its Spanish form ("Inter-District", "All-District", "Distrito Federal"). It does so whatever the sense: a named neighbourhood (Strip District, Garden District, Diamond District, red-light district), an administrative or court area (Water District, Port District, Northern District of Illinois, school district) or the title District Attorney. Other words for areas such as "neighborhood", "zone", "county" or "region" are not among its firings; the opposite pole takes "Zone" and the Chinese and Arabic words for area.

125801.title: The name "Gotham" in any sense
125801.explanation: The unit fires on the word "Gotham" itself, at the moment the name is complete (the token " Gotham", or the "am"/"ams" piece after "Goth"). It does not care what the name refers to: a publisher (Gotham Books), a record label, the Gotham typeface, the FOX television series, a pizza, a New York food market, the NJ/NY Gotham FC soccer club, the old New York Gothams baseball team, a property developer, or Gotham City in Batman plots. It is a reaction to the spelling of the name, not to a city, crime or superhero setting; other capitalised G-words split into pieces (Garmisch, Grampians, grimdark) belong to the opposite pole and do not fire it.

167009.title: City named in a formal name: City of London
167009.explanation: Fires on the token that completes a formal, multi-word city name, most strongly "London" right after "City of" (City of London Battalion, Choir, Regiment, Act, store) and "Brighton" right after "London," in the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. The same thing happens in Chinese on the city suffix after a city's name (伦敦城, 北京市民) and, more weakly, on "City" in "Gotham City". It reacts to the marked token in that fixed-name setting: plain mentions of London elsewhere in the same documents ("in London", "East London") do not produce the peak, and the opposite pole takes the Korean syllable 시 and 市/town in other uses.
key_words: london, brighton and south coast railway

188547.title: "Dent" in Harvey Dent; Batman villain names
188547.explanation: Fires most strongly on the surname token "Dent" right after "Harvey" in Batman material (district attorney Harvey Dent / Two-Face); all eight top plot-summary hits are exactly this. A weaker second group is other names from Batman's world read at the name token: Penguin, Riddler ("ler"), Ra's al Ghul ("'s"), Arkham ("ham"), Batsuit, No Man's Land, Heath Ledger as the Joker, and a look-alike "Harleen". It is a name-recognition unit tied to the token: in a long list of real people called Dent it peaks only on Harvey Dent, and ordinary first names of unrelated characters do not trigger it.

202487.title: Names and terms inside superhero-comics text
202487.explanation: The unit fires when the surrounding text is clearly about American superhero comics (DC or Marvel characters, series, casts and publication history) and the model is part-way through a name or term belonging to that world. The marked token itself varies: pieces of secondary characters and sidekicks (Bianca, Tommy Merlyn, Speedy, Sandy the Golden Boy, Gog, Robin, Scarecrow, Nora Fries), place or gadget names (Metropolis, Tumbler), people in credits and cast lists (Eric Nguyen, Eric Savin, Kimberly Brooks, Philip Proctor), and comics-format words (metaseries, anthology). So it reacts to the superhero-comics setting built up by the earlier text rather than to any one word; the same names or words such as Eric, Sandy, anthology or autumn in non-comics text would not be expected to fire it. Within that setting the choice of token is loose, so the pattern is a topic context more than a single precise trigger.

205442.title: "Red" and name fragments in superhero/sci-fi text
205442.explanation: The unit fires inside text about superhero comics, science fiction and horror, on the first piece of a genre name or term. The clearest group is the word "Red" opening a codename or comic-book term (Red Hood, Red Skull, Red Guardian, Red Kryptonite, Red Team, Red Queen, a red supergiant sun). A second group is the word piece "hor"/"or" (horror, horde, Strange Horizons, monorail), and a third is other fragments of invented or genre names in the same setting (Non-biological, Containment Unit, Comics, Committed to Arkham, Zod, climactic battle). It depends on the surrounding comics/sci-fi context: the word "red" or "horror" in ordinary non-genre prose is not what the examples show, so the unit is a mix of a context signal and a few favoured word pieces rather than one clean idea.

208075.title: The name "Joker" (and Cheshire Cat)
208075.explanation: The unit fires on the token "Joker" itself when it is used as a name, almost always the Batman villain ("the Joker", "The Joker's Asylum", "Joker-ized", cast and character lists) but also the film title "The Joker Is Wild" and Arthur naming himself "Joker". A second, weaker group is the "eshire" of "Cheshire Cat" in Alice in Wonderland plots, another grinning trickster figure, plus a few scattered proper names for sinister places after "the" ("the Hive", "The Pit") and "parasitic". It reacts to the name token, not to what follows; other Batman characters and villains named in the same sentences (Batman, Penguin, Two-Face, Harley Quinn, Riddler) do not set it off.

210632.title: Police complaints and bodies; the name Bruce Wayne
210632.explanation: The firings fall into two groups that share a police and crime setting. First, words for grievances and organisations in law-enforcement text: "complaint(s)" made to or against police (a trespassing complaint in a police blotter, complaints filed against officers, the site of a call-out), "misconduct" in public office, and names of police, fire or forensic bodies ("Police Chiefs Association", "IAFF", "IAI", "Northamptonshire Police"). Second, the first name "Bruce" when it is Bruce Wayne, Batman's civilian identity, usually where he is first named in a summary; a similar one-off is "Nikki" in Nikki Heat, a fictional detective. It reacts to the marked word itself in that setting; "complaint" in an ordinary consumer sense, or other first names, are not among the passages.

215865.title: Completed comic or cartoon franchise proper names
215865.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a well-known proper name from superhero comics or children's animation: "Wolverine", "X-Men", "Smallville", "Kim Possible", and in the plot summaries almost only the "ave" of "Batcave". It reacts to the marked token itself, once the name is recognisable as a famous character, team or place from that kind of franchise, whether it sits in running prose, a cast list or a programme list. Other names in the same texts (Storm, Magneto, Superboy, Gotham, Wayne Manor) do not trigger it, and the opposite pole of the neuron takes "Green Lantern", so it is a set of specific names rather than superhero text in general.

217862.title: Comic-book villain and place codenames from ordinary words
217862.explanation: Fires inside superhero-comic text (DC or Marvel articles, plot summaries, character lists) on the word piece that completes a codename or place name built from an everyday word: Penguin, Scarecrow, Killer Croc, Sentinel(s), Parasite, Master Man, Starman, the Raft prison, the Glades, Plateau City. Most are villains or adversaries named in passing, often in a list of foes the hero faces, plus a few fictional locations. It reacts to the marked token itself once the superhero setting is established; it does not fire on the lead heroes or on invented-sounding names (Wakanda, Diana, Black Panther are on the opposite pole), nor on the same words outside comics.

219037.title: Completing the name Cao Cao
219037.explanation: Fires on the last piece of the name "Cao Cao" (the "ao" of the second "Cao", or 曹 in Chinese text), the warlord of the late Han and Three Kingdoms period, in Wikipedia articles and film plots about that era. It reacts to the marked token itself as the completion of this particular, much-repeated personal name; related names nearby such as Cao Pi, Cao Song, Cao Wei, Liu Bei or Yuan Shao do not carry the peak. Much more weakly (about 0.6) it fires on "Bruce" in "Bruce Wayne", another central figure's given name, and there are stray firings on "Closure" in "Google Closure Compiler" and inside "Batarang" that do not fit.

227206.title: Word-piece inside a rare multi-piece name
227206.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a fragment in the middle (or at the first or last piece) of an unusual word or proper name that is split into several pieces, such as Audub-on (the most frequent case), Prim-ates, U-pan-ishads, Giraff-at-itan, Ich-ik-awa, G-ull-gentan, Vol-ta-ic, specios-s-issimus and Tenshit-achi. These are mostly foreign or transliterated names and Latin scientific names, with a loose lean towards natural-history text (birds, animals, dinosaurs), plus a dialect form (his'n) and a Latvian word in a code comment. In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on the first piece of coined or compound names (Bat-radia, Batwing, Man-Bat, Lex Luthor, Reese's, Cameron). Common words, and names that the model reads as a single familiar token, do not trigger it; the meaning of the surrounding passage matters little.

245694.title: Period after a paragraph or item number
245694.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the full stop (or closing bracket) that directly follows a number opening a new numbered paragraph, clause, rule, study question or footnote, as in "36.", "19.", "53." or "[12]". It is strongest in old books where a long run of consecutively numbered items has already gone by (verses, articles of an order, grammar rules, numbered sections), so the number is the next step in a running count and the item's text is about to begin. Numbers inside a sentence, such as dates, years, page references or quantities, do not trigger it, and ordinary sentence-ending full stops in plot summaries reach only about 0.3.

254112.title: Comic-book character names, especially animal-named villains
254112.explanation: The unit fires on a token inside or completing the name of a character from superhero comics, most often a villain's alias taken from an animal: Cheetah ("Cheet-ah"), Rhino, Catwoman ("Cat"), and also Titania, Terrigen, Fisk, Kato, Jameson, No Man's Land. It reacts to the marked name piece in a comics or superhero setting, where the surrounding text has already established Marvel or DC characters; the same pull toward animal nicknames shows in "tigers" (corrupt officials) and a film gangster called Cheetah. A weaker, loosely related tail has nothing to do with comics (a Russian word for bribery, the agency name R&AW, "all-source" intelligence, "cigarette filter", the band In Extremo), so the unit is not purely one idea, and ordinary personal names or animals in everyday text are not enough to fire it.

254826.title: Word-piece that continues or completes a rare name
254826.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a short word-piece in the middle or at the end of an uncommon proper name or rare word that the tokenizer has split up, in any script (Marc+ion, Apule+ius, Aëro+pe, Ald+o Bobadilla, Jack+y Lee, Marci+ão, Shres+hta, al+der, the 'о' inside Полоцкого, the 'ο' inside Ἀνάζαρβος). Most of the names are classical, early-Christian or foreign-language ones in encyclopedic lists, indexes and family tables. At about half strength it fires on the surname 'Dent' right after 'Harvey', the piece that completes a known two-part name. It does not fire on the first piece of a name, on common names written as one token, or on ordinary words; the meaning of the surrounding text does not matter.

317604.title: The syllable "Jia" in Chinese names
317604.explanation: The unit fires at full strength on the token "ia" that completes "Jia" in a Chinese name, most strongly when it is the first word of the document (Jia the anthropologist, Jia Hongsheng, Jia Yinghua) and more weakly later in a text (Jiajia, Jia-Shan Li, Jiaxing). So it reacts to the marked token and its spelling, not to the meaning of the passage. A much weaker second group, at about half strength or less, is a short one-syllable or single-letter name in a Chinese or Hong Kong setting and the small word right after it ("A" Ming, Sun "and" Aki, B "shot", Li"'s", Wang"'s", Tom "and" Jerry), and a third weak group is the preposition right after a sum of money ("$1 million from", "$1 million to", "$100,000 from", "$40,000 in cash from"). The firings in the plot summaries are all weak (0.36 or below) and belong to these loose groups; ordinary long Western names do not trigger it.

318922.title: Noun naming the space or group spanned
318922.explanation: Fires on the plain noun that names the enclosing space, playing area or collective that an action moves through or covers: "looked round the room", "limped about the room", "advance down the pitch", "dribble the length of the court", "led the field", "dusted the rafters", "around the house", "the rest of the group", "most of the crew", "others in the crowd", "his teammates", "all the class", "across the century", "throughout the air". The trigger is the marked word completing a phrase of traversal or extent (about/round/down/across/throughout/length of/rest of/all the + the + place or group); a second, related group is "season-best" and "program-best", where the peak is on "-best" after a noun naming the span being covered. It does not fire on the same nouns when they are simply a location ("in the room") without the sense of sweeping across or covering the whole, and named places after "all" ("all England") belong to the opposite pole.

324451.title: Last piece of the names Harley Quinn / Kauravas
324451.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the final piece that completes a particular multi-piece proper name. Two names dominate: "Quinn" right after "Harley" (the Joker's sidekick, in cast lists and plot sentences alike) and the ending "as" of "Kauravas" (the clan opposing the Pandavas in Mahabharata texts). Weaker firings are the closing piece of other rare transliterated names (Camassa-Holm, Huangdi Neijing, Ternate, Greek sphaira). It does not fire on the other names in the same lists (Joker, Bane, Robin, Pandavas) or on the first part of the name, so it is tied to these specific name endings rather than to villains or lists in general.

344071.title: Second half of a direction pair
344071.explanation: The strongest firings land on the word that names the opposite or returning direction of a two-sided flow, usually right after its partner has been stated or implied: incoming then "outgoing", inflow then "outflow", "two-way" street, "from/to", fromKey then "toKey", the giving side to the receiving side "of" the other, movements and counter-"movements", the value coming "in", outside looking "in", German "oder umgekehrt" (or the other way round), one half and the other "half". A weaker second group, which is the only kind seen in the plot summaries, is the time step that follows: "the next morning", "the following night", "the next day", often in "does not return by the next morning". It reads the meaning of the pairing, not one spelling; direction words used for travel tickets and fares (one-way fare, round trip, depart from) do not fire it and belong to the opposite pole.

346100.title: Last token completing a famous story-world name
346100.explanation: Fires on the token that completes the full name of a well-known character, place or company, usually at its first full mention in a plot summary or encyclopedia article: the surname or name ending in Bella Swan, Kate Austen, Naruto Uzumaki, Toshiro, Heihachi, Vlad Tepes, Mina Murray, Mark David Chapman; the place in Tatooine, Hill Valley, Judea, Leipzig; the company in Stark Industries and Wayne Enterprises. It reacts to the marked token as the point where a name becomes a recognisable specific entity, mostly from a famous fictional franchise and sometimes from history. It does not fire on the bare first name alone, on ordinary words, or on the kind of real-world venue and brand names (Asbury Park, Motorsports, Ritz) that drive the opposite pole.

347405.title: Names and labels of the good side
347405.explanation: It fires on the last piece of a name or label for someone or something on the honourable, defending or resisting side of a conflict. There are two groups: the "-ist" of "anti-fascist" / "antifascist" in accounts of wartime resistance groups, schools and writers, and the finishing piece of names of upright allies and their homes in fiction: Commissioner "Gordon", King "Kai", Ser Barristan Sel"my", Winter"fell", Aut"obot", Warriors of "Light", Ald"era"an, Elizabeth Pro"ctor", and the loyal Ming minister Shi Ke"fa". The unit reacts to the marked name piece itself, read in light of which side the bearer is on; names of villains and their henchmen (Bellatrix, Orochimaru, Bebop, Zola) do not fire it and belong to the opposite pole.

353620.title: Middle piece of an unfinished name or year
353620.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token as a word piece, not to the meaning of the passage: it fires partway through a word that the tokenizer has split and that is not yet complete. Two groups dominate: an inner fragment of an unusual, mostly foreign surname (Mas«l»any, Bus«l»je, Sejdi«ć», Des«isa», Lukas«iew»icz, Com«in», Vasili«y»evich) and the «0» of a year written as "June, 2006" or "January, 2019" right after a month and a comma. In the plot summaries it fires much more weakly on «Bat» as the opening piece of Batcave, Batmobile, Bat-Signal, Batgirl and "the Bat", and on the surname Vega. Common whole words and names that are complete in one token do not trigger it.

357872.title: Toxins, poisons and toxic substances
357872.explanation: The unit fires on words that name a poisonous or harmful substance: "toxins", "toxin", "toxic", "toxicology", "toxicologist", "poisons", "detoxifier", "toxic substances", harmful "chemicals", and the same words in Arabic and Chinese. The peak falls on the word piece that completes the idea ("-ology" after "toxic", "-isons" after "po", "substances" after "toxic"), so it is reacting to the meaning of the word just read. Most of the strongest cases are medical or biological (the liver clearing toxins, toxins in the blood, a toxicology report), and it fires in the same way on fictional poisons such as the Joker's toxin or Scarecrow's fear toxin. Other kinds of danger (bombs, wounds, disease) and drugs named without the sense of poison do not appear among its firings.

368887.title: Superhero-comics character code names being completed
368887.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes or makes recognisable the code name of a costumed hero or villain from the DC or Marvel superhero world: Rog-ues, Sh-az-am, To-omes, Elek-tra, the Wasp, Doctor Light, the Penguin, Metal-lo, the Vulture, the Phant-asm. It reacts to the name itself in a superhero setting, usually on its second word-piece, and also to franchise labels of the same world such as MCU and Kevin Feige. It does not fire on the names of the real writers and artists who make the comics (that is the opposite pole), nor on ordinary character names in non-superhero plots.

378497.title: Final piece completing a split-up proper name
378497.explanation: The unit fires on the later piece of a name or compound that the model reads in fragments, at the moment the piece makes the whole name recognisable: Cron+ulla, Gwy+dir, Leicester+Square / Leicester-square, WHB+Q, RCT+I, Cruc+ifer(ae), Sitt+ler, Dan+Reeves, the Chinese and Japanese place names 黄+阁 and 鶴+見, and in the plot summaries Bat-S+ignal and Bat+c(ave). Most are place names (several from New South Wales and London), with some broadcast call signs, a few people and hyphenated compounds such as to-night; it reacts to the completed name rather than to the meaning of the surrounding text. The passages are related but not one tight idea, and completions of foreign personal or cultural names (Kichak, Antar, Krays, Benno, Menorah, Röthlisberger) go to the opposite pole instead, so not every finished name triggers it.

394697.title: Pointing back to something just mentioned
394697.explanation: It fires at the end of a short phrase that refers back to a thing, act or statement the text has just set out: 'provides this', 'was included in this,', 'doing the latter,', 'do just that', 'paid no attention to this', 'achieve these ratios', 'followed her example', 'to realise this hope' (這希望), or a noun repeated with 'the' after its first mention (the recording, the box, the ring, the board, the garland). The trigger is the meaning of the preceding text, a back-reference being completed, usually as the object of a verb such as do, use, achieve, provide or follow; the marked token varies and is sometimes the comma or 'by'/'before' that follows the reference. The same words where they introduce something new are not among the strong passages, and the weaker plot-summary peaks (unorthodox, underhandedly, slow) do not fit the pattern.

407102.title: Final piece that completes a surname or name
407102.explanation: Fires on the last token of a multi-piece proper name, at the moment the name becomes complete: mostly surnames (Bonap-arte, Barn-ave, Mor-ris, Mar-bury, Flamm-ang, Van Cle-ef, Dant-ec, Jär-vi, Bea-umont, Bul-lock, Sion-is, B-atts) and also band or act names in lists (Girl-pool, Mouse On Mars, Majid Jordan) and a few named things (Bats-uit, the Nar-rows, Black Mask). It reacts to the name-ending token itself in any language (Russian, Spanish, English), not to what the surrounding text is about. It does not fire on the first piece of a name, on first names, or on ordinary words that are not finishing a name.

410913.title: Recurring topic noun or name, mentioned again
410913.explanation: The unit fires on a noun or proper name that the document has already used several times and that names its main subject or setting, at the moment it comes up again: "boiler" in articles about boilers, "fingers" in a passage about lost fingers, "car" in a car article, "glass" for a glass company, "anthropology" for an anthropologist, "New York", "Idaho", "Army", "crew", "trousers", and "Gotham" (or "Simba") in the plot summaries. The repeated word is usually the expected piece of a familiar phrase ("boiler drum", "flat glass", "City of New York", "Social anthropology", "prime crew", "Gotham Zoo"). It reacts to the marked token as a re-mention of an established topic term, not to any one word; a first mention of a new noun or name, or an incidental noun unrelated to the document's subject, does not fire it.

427568.title: Names of invented towns, cities and countries
427568.explanation: The unit fires when a story's setting is an invented place: on the word "fictional"/"fictitious" itself, on the generic noun that follows it ("fictional city", "fictional nation", "fictitious country of"), or on the place-type part of a made-up name (Metro City, Pelton University, Llanview, Weatherfield, Metroville, Gotham City). It is reacting to the meaning "this place is made up for the story", usually near the start of a plot summary where the setting is introduced, and it often peaks just before or on the invented name. Real places (Savannah, Los Angeles, Tacoma) and ordinary workplaces or businesses do not trigger it.

435478.title: Superhero-comics character and team names
435478.explanation: Fires on the token that completes a proper name from superhero comics (a Marvel or DC character, team or shared universe) once the text has made clear it is about a comic-book franchise: Agents of Atlas, Dark Phoenix, Phoenix Force, Arrowverse, Killer Frost, Jennifer Walters, Maya Lopez, Harley Quinn, Green Goblin, Edward Nygma, Jean Grey, She-Hulk, Azrael, Selina Kyle. It also fires on "mantle" when a character takes on a hero identity (the mantle of Nightwing, of Batgirl). It reacts to the name being recognised in that setting, not to the bare word: the peaks are ordinary words or surnames (Atlas, Frost, Grey, Walters, Force) that carry this meaning only because the comics context precedes them, and actor names, creators and plot events in the same passages are not where it peaks.

438070.title: Repeated name of the text's main organisation or figure
438070.explanation: The unit fires on the name (usually its last or identifying piece) of the organisation, community or person the passage is about, when that name comes up again after many earlier mentions: Citi in the Citibank article, Animal Outlook, the New York Fed, Chabad, Grassroots Leadership, Fitch, the Ismaili community, the people of Bahá, the World Food Programme and the Presbyterian Church in Chinese, and persons such as Gallatin, Li Deyu, Shivaji and Batman. It is strongest when the name stands as an actor or as a label attached to something else ('Chabad spokesman', 'Fitch-rated', 'Springfield Police Officer', 'Ismaili Council', 'Shivaji's office'). It reacts to the marked name itself in its context as the established subject; most are institutions or organised groups, with protagonists of biographies and plots as a weaker second group. A group referred to only in general terms ('our values', 'we as a profession') belongs to the opposite pole, and a name mentioned once in passing does not fire it.

453490.title: Closing piece of a split name or set phrase
453490.explanation: Fires on the piece that finishes a word or stock phrase already under way, where the ending could be guessed from what came before; it reacts to the form being completed, not to a topic. One group is the last piece of a long foreign surname or learned term that is split into several tokens (Zaitse-v / Zaytse-v, Pleist-ocene, Mezent-ius, Peg-ler, Ritch-ie, Schiapare-lli, Gund-erson, Bello-q), strongest when the same name has already appeared earlier in the list or article. The other group is the expected second half of a fixed pairing (counter-battery, point to point, playing to capacity, a snatch of, the best he can to, staff member, party guests, sunroof, co-publisher). The peaks sit on the closing piece, not on the opening piece of the name or on freely chosen words, and the passages share no common subject.

458118.title: Word-piece that makes a longer name recognisable
458118.explanation: This unit reacts to the marked token itself: a later piece of a multi-piece proper name or specialist term, at the point where the name becomes recognisable but the full phrase is usually not finished yet (Potawat-omi [Nation], soprano sax-[ophonist], South London [Theatre], World Golf Championship [title], Ark-ham [Knight], krypton-ite, Crime Alley, Aztec in Chinese). The passages fall into loose groups: instrument words in musician biographies (sax, saxophone, tuba), place-based names (South London, Crime Alley, Arkham), and rare or foreign names split into pieces (Sergyeyev, Roscioli, O'Malley, Kaldur, Pueblo chico). It does not depend on the topic of the text, and it does not fire on the first piece of a name or on ordinary whole words, so the grouping is by token position inside a name rather than by meaning.

465171.title: Piece that completes a multi-part name
465171.explanation: The unit fires on the token that finishes a name or fixed term spelled over several pieces: the last word-piece of a brand, organisation, software package or chemical (Kidz-Search, Add-gene, TI-B-ASIC, SitePr-ism, Martind-ale, Water-stones, EC-PI, tert-butyllith-ium, drf-yas-g, Common\Collections, cms.api) or the last word of a set phrase (UK Data Archive, duplicate code, transfection reagent). It reacts to the marked token itself in its role of closing the name, and is strongest when the name is the subject of the document and has already been written out earlier. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on the final piece of names such as League of Shadows, GCPD, Ra's al Ghul, Hugo Strange and Lucius Fox. It does not fire on the first piece of such a name, on ordinary single-token words, or on plain word endings in French or Arabic text.

485574.title: Later word-piece of a split-up proper name
485574.explanation: The strongest firings land on a middle or final word-piece of a name that the model reads in several fragments, at the point where the name becomes recognisable: the "rank" of Ivano-Frankivsk (four separate passages), the "ani" of Asrani, the "av" of Cernavoda, the "ler" of Riddler, the "girl" of Batgirl, and the "udence" of prudence. It reacts to the marked token as a piece of spelling, not to the meaning of the scene, and it does not fire on the first piece of such a name or on names written as one whole token. A weaker and scattered second group falls on ordinary whole words (norms, of, distract, dark, around, entertaining, hunting) that share no clear idea, so the unit is only partly explained.

496782.title: End of a remark inside an itemised listing
496782.explanation: The unit fires in long, repetitive listings where every entry carries a short comment: a round-by-round fantasy football draft, game-by-game and week-by-week season summaries, publishers' book advertisements with press quotes, a picture gallery catalogue, a roster of lodges, a numbered list of topics or songs. The peak usually falls where one entry's remark closes or pauses, on the full stop, comma, question mark or closing quotation mark ("over and over again."—Chicago Evening Post), and sometimes on a word inside the remark ("advantage", "dedicated", "section", "for"). It is driven by the list-entry format before the token rather than by any particular word, and the pattern is loose; ordinary continuous narrative such as plot summaries barely moves it (0.28 at most).

504207.title: Expected head word arriving after its modifier
504207.explanation: Fires on the word that fills a slot the preceding words have just opened, usually the head word straight after a modifier or a set-up verb: 'Kennedy's successor', 'the old synonym', 'an old Latin root', 'the English name', 'fair prices', 'perfectly cooked', 'spell correctly', 'would-be tacklers', 'pointed towards the killer', 'find the murderer', 'more nearly true than'. Two loose clusters stand out among these: words about language itself (synonym, root, name, way of writing, mistranslation, spelling, deciphers, perfect English, a good poem) and the person a hunt or rivalry is aimed at (killer, murderer, crook, enemies, successor). It reacts to the anticipated word landing rather than to one subject, so it is a mixed unit; the modifier itself and the same words used without such a set-up are not what is marked.

515413.title: Participle after a noun: caused by, provided by
515413.explanation: The unit reacts to grammar, not to a topic. It fires on the verb of a short describing clause attached to a noun, usually a past participle that says where the thing came from or who made it: "deficiencies occasioned by", "the fire caused by", "conditions laid down by", "exemption provided by", "questions arising out of", "powers that belonged to". The peak is on the participle itself or on the small word that follows it (by, in, down), just before the agent or source is named, and the same construction triggers it in Arabic, Korean and Chinese. In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on the same shape ("bombs hidden around", "a shipment that belonged to", "a helicopter sent by", "a wound he received"); the main verb of a sentence, with nothing being described by it, does not show up.

541023.title: Next item in a long list repeating a stem
541023.explanation: Fires deep inside long enumerations and catalogues (index entries, lists of programmes, book titles, associations, dated events, items separated by commas) whose items keep reusing the same head words, in any language. The peak falls early in a new item, on the token where it repeats or slightly varies the shared stem: 'Falkland Islands F[alk]land Islands Association', 'THE LITTLE COLONEL[,] MAID OF HONOR', 'Jordan[ian] Writers Association', 'people with [disabilities] who', 'The [Blue] Card-Lissner ... Program', or a small joining word inside such a list ('by', 'with', 'and', '/'). It reacts to the list-like, repetitive setting rather than to any one word; ordinary narrative prose barely moves it, and in plot summaries it only fires weakly on the second word of a name that recurs through the text (Gotham 'City', Bruce 'Wayne').

552240.title: End of a table cell before the next
552240.explanation: The unit fires at the boundary where one cell of a table ends and the next is about to begin, most strongly in Wikipedia table markup: the line break after the last column heading (ISBN, Round, Votes, Release Date) or after a number in a results row, and the "||" separator after a figure in a statistics row. The same happens in a markdown table header in source code and in a flattened table of figures in a book, so it tracks the tabular layout rather than any particular word. Much more weakly (about half strength or less) it fires on the full stop that closes a long sentence in a plot summary, which looks like the same 'one unit finished, next one starts' signal; ordinary mid-sentence text and commas do not trigger it.

561621.title: Word closing a descriptive phrase mid-sentence
561621.explanation: No single topic or word drives this unit; the pattern is loose and mostly about sentence position. It fires on the word that finishes a short descriptive phrase inside a longer sentence that is clearly going to carry on: the noun closing a count in sports biographies ("started seven of 13 games", "9 of the final 10 contests"), or a participle or adjective giving a state or manner ("the street deserted", "unchaperoned", "Barely literate", "though conducted", "was completed", "does not want to inherit"). About a third of the strongest passages do not fit this (a comma, "and", "has", the opening word "Driving", a Japanese verb ending), so the reading is tentative; the same words at the end of a finished sentence or in plain narration of actions do not stand out.

604205.title: Last piece of a name filling an object slot
604205.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a name or fixed compound term, most often the final sub-word piece of a name split into several pieces (Kog-oro, Lionbl-aze, Svid-ler, Har-uno, O'Le-ary, Per-i, quadr-angle, P-DL, co-driver, major leagues, position player). The name nearly always sits in a complement position: the last item of a list of names, or the thing named right after a verb or preposition such as 'and', 'with', 'to', 'in the', 'on' (in the plot summaries: 'assault on Batman', 'lure Batman', 'convince Batman', 'Nightwing', 'O'Neil'). It reacts to the marked token as the point where the name is finished, not to any topic; the subject matter ranges over anime plots, Mars geography, chess and sport. A name at the start of a sentence acting as the subject, or the earlier pieces of a name, do not show up among the peaks, and the pattern is loose rather than sharp.

830265.title: Costumed-superhero name stems, especially Bat- and Wayne
830265.explanation: The unit fires inside superhero text on the tokens that name a costumed hero, his civilian identity or his branded gear. The strongest cases are the 'Bat' stem (Batgirl, Batmobile, Batcave, Batsuit, Bat Family, Bat Lady), 'Wayne' in Bruce Wayne, and Daredevil / Matt Murdock, with Spider-Man, Mutant Ninja Turtles, Ororo and 'secret' identities also appearing. A few weaker peaks land on ordinary words or commas (',', 'same', 'his') inside the same kind of superhero plot, so the context matters as well as the token. It does not fire on cosmic or space-opera comic material (that is the opposite pole) or on names in non-superhero stories.

830342.title: Superhero screen adaptations and their cast credits
830342.explanation: The unit fires in text about DC and Marvel superhero characters at the point where a screen version is named or credited to an actor: 'voiced by', 'portrayed by', the actor's name in brackets after a character (Kevin Conroy as Batman), and franchise labels such as 'DC Extended Universe' and 'Marvel Cinematic Universe'. It also fires, a little less, on the first character names or cast list of a superhero film (Adrian Toomes, Richard Parker, the Watchmen cast, 'one of four villains' in Spider-Man: Homecoming). It depends on the superhero-franchise setting: in an actor's biography the long list of ordinary film and television roles does not set it off, only the superhero film does, and the comic-book publication history of a character is not what it marks.

833184.title: Ford car models and characters' signature items
833184.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes or specifies a well-known named thing. The strongest group is the model name straight after the make "Ford" (Ford GT, Ford GT40, Ford Zephyr, Ford roadster). The second group is the trademark names and props of comic-book and film characters and of brands: the Spirit's costume, the Batmobile, the Lazarus Pit, the smiley-face badge, the Joker's trademark toxin, the two-headed coin, a costume of red, yellow and purple rags, Copperhead, Coca-Cola Classic, and the second half of a person's name (Thomas Wayne, Ben Johnson, Robert Duvall, Doc White). It does not fire on cars, costumes or names in general, only where a specific, recognisable model or signature item is being named; a few passages ("temperance", "banned") do not fit.

833700.title: Star Wars factions: Empire, Alliance, Federation, Death Star
833700.explanation: Fires inside Star Wars text, in any language, on the names of the story's warring powers and their forces: Imperial, Empire, Rebel Alliance, Rebellion, Trade Federation, First Order, stormtrooper, clone army. It also fires on the small word just before such a franchise term is due ("the" / "of" before Death Star, "a" before blockade or weakness) and on the stolen "plans". It reacts to the Star Wars war-and-politics setting rather than to one spelling; other Star Wars items such as lightsabers do not drive it (they belong to the opposite pole), and every strong passage is Star Wars, so plain uses of "imperial" or "alliance" elsewhere are not shown to fire it.

839883.title: The Joker and clownish comic figures
839883.explanation: The unit fires on the word Joker when it names Batman's clown villain, in plots, cast lists, voice credits and comic titles alike. More weakly it fires on words with the same clown or jester sense: Clown as a role in Batman Returns, comic in 'comic relief' or 'tragic or comic', funhouse, and other gimmick villains from the same rogues' gallery (Riddler, Mad Hatter). It reacts to the marked word itself in that sense, not to villains in general: Batman, Bane, Penguin or other characters named nearby do not carry the peak.

842440.title: The word "vigilante": crime-fighting outside the law
842440.explanation: The unit fires on the first piece of the word "vigilante" ("vigil"), in plots and articles where a private person takes the law into his own hands against criminals: becoming a vigilante, a vigilante group, vigilante killings, a masked vigilante. It reacts to the marked word together with the idea, since a few weaker firings land on other words with the same sense of crime control outside the regular police: "privatized" prisons after a rise in crime, a zero-tolerance "Police and Crime Commissioner" (PCC), and a Hindi gloss for people who fight criminals illegally. Ordinary violence, weapons or police work without the idea of self-appointed justice does not fire it (the opposite pole takes "assault" rifles and attacks).
key_words: takes the law into his own hands

886609.title: Verb arriving after a long, tangled lead-in
886609.explanation: The unit fires on the word that picks a sentence back up after a long or awkward stretch with no comma, most often the main verb that finally arrives after a heavy subject or a fronted phrase ("...Charles, Michael and Jane help", "the gang war between the rival gang of Parshuram Shiva rocked", "over all the emperor sent", "this speech of his betrays", "the next flare was"), or a small linking word right after it ("is an", "wor as mad", "in awe upon"). It reacts to the sentence structure before the marked token, not to any particular word or topic. The pattern is loose: several strong passages are mid-word pieces in Hindi text and a Ruby "merge!" call, which do not fit, and in the plot summaries it fires only weakly on ordinary verbs in later clauses (comforts, relocates, appears, returns, exclaims). A verb that follows a short, plain subject does not set it off.

902490.title: Digit after 65/67 in serial numbers; list fillers
902490.explanation: The clearest group is a digit inside a multi-digit number in a running series of dates, issue numbers, page numbers or order numbers, and almost always the digit that follows "65" or "67" (1674, Executive Order 674, issues 659-662, p. 673, 65690, #654, and 6,750 written out in Chinese); other numbers in the same lists do not fire. A second, looser group is a middle token of an item in a long repetitive list or of a line of rhymed verse: a road or village suffix in Chinese lists of stops and villages, part of a lake name, "Regiment" in a repeated unit name, or a line-opening word in a ballad or refrain. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on a pronoun or name that refers back to a character just mentioned (him, her, whom, who, Joker). These groups do not reduce to one idea; the marked token itself, in a formulaic sequence, seems to matter more than the meaning.

904823.title: Word right after a singular "the"-name
904823.explanation: It fires on the small word or punctuation mark that comes straight after a single named thing that carries the definite article: "The Broadway", "The Groove begins", "the Illawalla's", "the Purandar dates", "The Condroz is a", German "Der Raichberg ist eine", "the Phantasm, a". The unit is reacting to the text before the marked token (a name or coined title with "the" has just ended and the sentence is about to say what it is or does), so the peak lands on a linking verb, a possessive 's, a comma, or the "a"/"of" that opens the description. It does not fire the same way after plural "the" names such as team or group names ("The Tampico Stogies are", "the Mustangs"), which belong to the opposite pole, and it is weak in the plot summaries (at most about a third of its maximum).

910564.title: Small index number inside a letter-number label
910564.explanation: The unit fires on a small number (mostly 1, 2 or 3) that is glued to a letter or short code to form a designation: To2-To3, F3, C1, g1, T3 tram line, V1-V2, P2-P5, S16, X18+, LP1, sudok1. It also fires on the same thing spelled out in other scripts or languages (Chinese 一 in 'Xiaohu First Bridge', Japanese リー ending 'S-three', Icelandic 'einn'), and weakly on other numbering tokens such as 'Ares III', 'February 2' and 'once more'. It reacts to the marked token itself in its role as an index in a series of labelled items, often when a sibling label (C0, To2, V1) has just been named; ordinary quantities, years, scores and measurements do not appear among its strong passages. A couple of top passages ('SS1 and her', 'June 1 through') peak just after such a number rather than on it.

911984.title: No clear pattern: codes, wing labels, fragments
911984.explanation: I could not find one idea behind this unit. The strongest firings fall into loosely related groups: a digit or letter inside a model number, ratio or registry code ("1.50:1", "1500", "140hp", "L67", "L0272", "Division 25"); the words "left" and "right" used as political wing labels ("Left Wing Section", "left faction", "to its right"); path or host name parts in configuration code ("media", "_static"); and stray pieces of names and words ("Legion of Honour", "Lucifer", "liturgy", "Falangist", "OAS"). The most that they share is that the marked token sits inside a fixed designation or label, and in the plot summaries the unit is weak (under half strength) and lands on unrelated name pieces such as "Legion", "Axis", "Jean-Paul", "Knightfall" and "Two-Face".

919295.title: The digit 8 ending a number
919295.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the digit "8" written as the last piece of a number or identifier, most strongly in years ending in 38 (1138, 1338, 1738), and also in 1986 and 1989, in the Go type name Int8 (reflect.Int8, Int8Option) and in the car name Audi R8. Other final digits in similar dates mostly do not fire it (the opposite pole takes years ending in 0, 5 or 6), although a few weaker hits fall on other digits (1275, 1939, an ISBN) and one on the word "test". In the plot summaries only "1986" is a clear case; the remaining weak firings on words about Bruce Wayne's background (after, his, billionaire, Thomas) look unrelated.

920688.title: Mid-phrase linking words; no single idea
920688.explanation: I could not find one idea. The peaks fall on small connecting words or word-pieces in the middle of a plain everyday phrase, just before an almost determined completion ("have sex with [her]", "one drink a [day]", "Buys a [Loaf]", "choking on [an olive]", "salt on your [fish]", "jobs to [fill]", "recognized him as [one of]"). There are loose tilts toward food and drink (drink, loaves, wine, olive, fish, smurfberries), toward counted quantities (100,000 tickets, 500 guests, the most, thousands) and toward things one character says, asks or offers another, but none of these holds across the list, and the plot-summary firings are weak and scattered (wear, arrive, from, accepted, injuries, thousands, onto). Activations are all bunched between 0.84 and 1.00 with no clear topic, so this looks like a diffuse unit rather than a concept.

926177.title: Going into a river, lake or floodwater
926177.explanation: The unit fires on the word for a body of water (river, lake, stream, water, sea, loch) at the moment someone or something physically goes into it, comes out of it or has to get across it: soldiers or cavalry wading into a ford, a bull plunging into the stream, a monster rising from or retreating into the lake, grenades thrown into the river. A closely related group is water that is high or "swollen" by rain so that a river cannot be forded or a place is flooded; in the plot summaries this shows up more weakly as flooded arenas and tunnels, sewers, and people falling into the water. It reacts to the situation (a body entering or crossing inland water, or water risen in flood) rather than to any mention of water: sea voyages, drinking water or a river named only as a location do not appear among the strong firings.

940900.title: A number that continues a running series
940900.explanation: Fires on, or on the word right after, a number that is one item in a running series or is set against an earlier number in the same text: chapter numerals ("xix ... xx.", "Chap. x."), chart positions ("#14 ... but #2 on"), a second figure after a first ("fifty-one ... forty of", "Twenty-Three ... Twenty-One"), numbered items ("COP 1 ... COP 2 took", "jScrollPane1 =", "a second series") and the last digit of a year inside a date range or chronology ("between 1931 and 1935 ... in 1933", "between 1940 and 1942"). The number can be digits, a Roman numeral, a spelled-out number or an ordinal, so it is reacting to the position in a count or sequence, not to a particular word. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on the last digit of a year that dates a new step of the story ("In 1978", "By 1980") and on "once more". The pattern is loose: it is a general "this is the next number in the list" response rather than one sharp topic.

967057.title: X-Men's Xavier and psychic mutant powers
967057.explanation: The unit fires most strongly in superhero-comics text about the X-Men: on the name Xavier (Charles Xavier, Professor X, the Xavier Institute), on X-Men members such as Archangel, and on words for mind powers (telepathic, telekinetic, psychic, using her mind) in stories about mutants or psychic creatures. These are two related groups: X-Men proper names, and psychic or telepathic abilities of super-powered characters. More weakly it fires on the civilian names of other comic-book characters (Bruce Wayne, Barbara Gordon, Ben Urich, Adrian Veidt). It does not fire on ordinary people's names or on mental words outside a superhero or supernatural-power setting.

989429.title: Superhero's double identity: civilian linked to hero persona
989429.explanation: The unit reacts to the meaning of the text before the peak: a superhero story has reached the point where an ordinary person and a costumed hero are tied together as one. It fires on the linking words of phrases such as "doubles as the flying hero", "a secret double life as a masked vigilante", "moonlights as", "as Superman,", "civilian alter ego" and "adopting the alias Spider-Man", and just as strongly when someone finds out who the hero is ("deduces Spider-Man's secret identity", "deduces that Matt is Daredevil", "learns Rick is Dragonfly", "unless Batman reveals his identity"). A weaker second group is other superhero-origin material, such as a list of newly gained powers (flight, x-ray vision, superhuman strength) or a later mention of the hero's name. It does not fire on ordinary uses of "as", "is" or "secret" outside a hero-with-a-hidden-identity setting, and one stray source-code passage looks unrelated.

994890.title: Short name confirmed, not its longer look-alike
994890.explanation: The unit fires on the token right after a name, code or identifier that has a longer near-twin elsewhere in the same text, at the moment the next token shows the name stopped at the shorter form. Examples: "Highway 28 near" in an article about Highway 28A, "NY 8 north" beside NY 80, "DEL club" beside DEL2, "P30 models" beside P30 Pro, "VFR400 to" beside VFR400R, "Ashley." beside Ashley 2, "1.6–" after 1.64, chord "B–" after B♭, and in code "eval``" after eval_, "I," beside Ip, "resp.get" beside resp_data, "user.create" beside userDB, "SldGwtService.class" beside SldGwtServiceAsync. The marked token itself is arbitrary (a preposition, a dash, a bracket, a method call such as .create or .get); what matters is that it closes off the base name. It does not fire on the longer variant itself or on an ordinary repeated name that has no confusable sibling; the plot-summary hits are weak (Joker beside Jokerz, Discovery's beside Discovery One).

1006752.title: Fictional companies and newspapers in franchise universes
1006752.explanation: Fires at the moment the text names a made-up institution that belongs to a superhero or other franchise universe: most strongly on "Daily" when it is about to become the Daily Bugle or Daily Planet, and on the company word in Wayne Enterprises, Sacks Industries, LuthorCorp, Anaheim Electronics, or right after "chief executive officer of" in a character biography. A weaker, related group is other in-universe invented things (a fictional book inside Harry Potter, "in-universe", "within the series"). It depends on the preceding context being a comic-book, game or franchise story; a real newspaper or real company in ordinary text does not appear among its strong passages, and the opposite pole fires on real-world named things such as Apollo or the International Space Station.

1021040.title: Midway through a stock compound phrase
1021040.explanation: The unit fires on the first or middle piece of a familiar fixed expression, just before the word that completes it: "single" in "as a single parent/father/mother" (and "on" in "raising them on her own"), "comic" before "strip", "conduction" before "band", "manga adaptation", "pop-ups", "lif" in "lifeline", "Dailies". The clearest repeated case is a widowed or divorced character left to raise children alone; a looser group is comics and adaptations, and two passages are the wedding at Cana (stone jars, "the mother of Jesus"). It reacts to being inside a predictable set phrase, not to one topic, so the pattern is mixed; the same words standing alone ("single" meaning unmarried, a finished noun phrase) do not appear among the strong firings.

1042958.title: Changing suffix in a series of codes
1042958.explanation: Fires on the small piece of a label that changes from one entry to the next in a run of similar codes or names: the letters of a model code (3FN after 2RH, 2RJ and so on; Xeon 7120N after 7110N, 7110M), the suffix of a template or program field name (r_head_label, leader2_type, placeofburial_label, AddStdLevel, MATCH-OUTPUT-FILE), or the number or letter of a numbered entry (Volume 2, 765a, C 4 b, 8d, set number 7884, 8266). It needs a list-like setting in which several parallel identifiers have just been read; it reacts to the position in that pattern, not to a particular letter or digit, and it does so in source code, infoboxes, catalogues and Chinese or Japanese lists alike. Ordinary story prose barely moves it: in the plot summaries the strongest firing is a third of the maximum and falls on unrelated words. The opposite pole fires on similar-looking figure and section suffixes ('Fig. 3d', 'Part II'), so the exact boundary between the two poles is not clear from these passages.

1049878.title: Real name of a superhero-universe character
1049878.explanation: Fires in Marvel and DC text at the point where a character's civilian or real name is given, usually on the end of the surname or on the punctuation that links it to the alias: Mac Gargan, John Walker, Jennifer Walters / She-Hulk, Scott Summers/Cyclops, Carol Danvers, Barbara Gordon / Batgirl, Barry Allen / Flash, Thunderball (Eliot Franklin), Clark Kent, Lex Luthor, Bruce Wayne. A weaker second group is the article or word just before a codename or the label 'supervillain' ('the Thinker', 'the Green Goblin', 'as the masked vigilante'), so the common thread is the pairing of a person's name with a comic-book identity. It needs the superhero setting; ordinary people's names in non-comics text, and technical prose (the opposite pole is chemistry articles), do not trigger it.

1053109.title: Just after a name missing from the text
1053109.explanation: Fires a token or two after a hole in the text where a name or word has been dropped, so the sentence reads as broken: "released by Records", "signed a record deal with Records, LLC", "It bypasses station, which closed permanently in", "the first ship of the class", "The city hired Corp Inc.", a filmography entry with only "(1964)" and no title, and Chinese sentences whose place or sponsor name is gone ("至段", "由所贊助", "舊址"). A second, related group is the first words of a document that starts in mid-sentence. It reacts to the missing piece before the marked token, not to the marked token itself, which is an ordinary comma, full stop, "in", "Records" or "class"; the same words in complete sentences with the name present do not fire it. A few weaker passages (a list of Vogue editions, a parenthetical "particularly, but") show no gap and fit only loosely, and the plot-summary firings are very weak.

1067286.title: DC and Marvel comic-character franchise write-ups
1067286.explanation: The unit fires inside encyclopedia-style text about superhero comic-book franchises (DC Comics, Marvel, the Arrowverse, the MCU, the DC Extended Universe, the Arkham games): pages saying a show or film is "based on" DC or Marvel characters, cast and character lists, and notes about which version of a character appears in which adaptation. It reacts to the surrounding subject rather than to one word: the peak falls on a small word just before a character or title is named ("based on", "a variation of the", "as the", "featuring the", "In a mid-credits scene, an") or on a franchise name itself (Barbara, Gordon, Luthor, Lane, Bullock, Hush, Grayson, Danvers, CBR.com). The same words and the same kind of cast list or plot summary for ordinary films, with no comic-book universe in view, do not fire it.

1068129.title: Category word introducing a set of items
1068129.explanation: The unit fires on a word that names a set of things belonging to the topic, at the point where that set is about to be listed or spelled out. One group is section headings that open a roster in reference articles: "Personnel" after a track listing, "Current squad" for a football club, Spanish "Formación" for a band line-up, the label "Nutrition Information". The other group is expository prose naming a topic's features before describing them: "the functions of the chief executive", "the symptoms of decompression sickness", "the most common symptoms", "periodic trends such as", "logical behavior is defined by", "three types of reaction", "habits students are working on", "functionals of the density". It does not fire on the listed items themselves, and it is weak in story text, where it only reaches the stock line "an ensemble of characters from the history of ..."; the link between the two groups is loose, so this is a broad pattern rather than a sharp one.

1079880.title: Token inside a recognisable set term or name
1079880.explanation: The unit fires on a token that is one piece of a fixed, recognisable label: a technical term, a class code, a title or a proper name. Most often the term echoes one the document has already used or its own subject ("O5" after O2-O4 in the O-type star article, "digraphs", "metal-thallium-boron" after nickel-boron, "concurrency" after repeated "runs concurrently", "first named storm", "No Means No" for the band Nomeansno, "third generation", Chinese "不送气"), or it is a well-known title or name ("Name That Tune", "Mass in B minor", "Columbus Catholic High School", "Killer Croc", "Buzz Lightyear", "Neo Joker", "Batman: Arkham Knight"). It is found in encyclopedic, list-like text and reacts to the term being recognised as a set expression, not to any one word; ordinary narrative words and freely chosen wording do not trigger it. The idea is fairly broad, and a few peaks (a year digit in "1971", "playable", "resulting") fit only loosely.

1113807.title: No clear pattern; connecting words after odd wording
1113807.explanation: I could not find one idea. The peaks are almost all plain connecting tokens: 'with', 'to', 'that', 'an', 'its', 'towards', a past-tense ending, commas and full stops, and most lie within the first lines of a text fragment that starts mid-sentence. About half come right after wording that is slightly off: a dropped word ('a small white belonging to', '( level data items)', '3.844 公里'), a misspelling ('Neplease ethnic'), foreign or odd names ('morie tonger,', ''S Make It', 'California University of Los Angeles'), or a garbled phrase ('loomed to within its first hour'). The rest are ordinary sentences ('piled high with baskets', 'unscrewed', 'undismayed,'), so this is a tentative reading and not a subject, scene or particular word.

1120499.title: Text with a missing word or glitch
1120499.explanation: The unit fires at a spot where the text is defective: a word has been dropped and left a gap or double space ("made a  of 129", "This  creates", "was a  paddle frigate", "account of the  mutiny", "task force to teaching", "California  Diego Valley"), the grammar is broken ("The man is represent himself", "sighin' grateful"), or a number or abbreviation is oddly written or cut ("1817-'8", "75°—100°", "100,000 cash prize" with no currency sign, year ranges like "680–86"). The peak sits on the token right after the hole or on the malformed piece itself. In the plot summaries it fires almost only on the name "R. F." split across a sentence break ("...to R." / "F. approves"). Clean, complete sentences with ordinary names and numbers do not trigger it; a few firings ("Narayana", a Chinese year) show no obvious defect.

1121133.title: Group noun naming who qualifies; appositive commas
1121133.explanation: There is no single clean idea; the firings fall into three loose groups. The strongest is a plain noun naming a class of people by sex, age or status (low-income women, girls, women, a woman, boys, regions) at the point where the text says who may apply, join, enlist, be covered or be excluded, just before the qualifying detail ("girls aged between", "Boys were excluded if"). A second group is the comma after a place or a person that is about to be specified ("Savannah, Georgia", "Hyannis, Massachusetts", "her father, a police officer", "Dick Grayson, the youngest member"), and a third is the closing word of a set compound (cpu_count, life story, mortal remains, month of birth, pumpkin). In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, mostly on the name of a young ward or trainee (Dick, Jean-Paul, Cranston); ordinary mentions of people or places with nothing left to specify do not fire it.

1129939.title: Reusing an already-defined name in code
1129939.explanation: Fires almost only in source code (Python, JavaScript, Go, PHP, Ruby, Java), at the point where a statement plugs in something already established a few lines earlier: a local variable, parameter, attribute or index that was just defined or just used in a parallel line and is now passed as an argument or subscript (raw_csv, locator_type, kernel_h, parseFn, $dependencies, &meta, match[2], m[6], search_model.offset), or the closing '();' and line break that finish such a short, predictable statement. It reacts to the text before it being a slot whose filler is copied from context, not to any particular spelling; definitions of new names, comments and docstrings do not fire it. In prose it is much weaker and shows the same back-reference shape: an object pronoun or repeated word pointing to someone or something just named ('kill him', 'give her', 'creative director', 'crew members'), and in Japanese the stock completion of a phrase used just before.

1159446.title: Villain and hero as stock story roles
1159446.explanation: Fires on the word that names a stock character of melodrama or comic-book fiction, above all "villain" (villainess, villains, villainy, supervillain, "Heroes and Villains", "Wicked"), and less strongly "hero", "superhero" and "DC" Comics. It is strongest when the text talks about the role itself as a convention: "stereotypical villain music", "like the villain of melodrama", "the villain always triumphs", "the villain of her piece", or someone "dramatically" dropping dead. In the plot summaries it fires at the opening of superhero stories on "Batman", "Robin", "Gotham" and "Batarang", where the costumed hero-versus-villain genre is being set up. It does not fire on plain accounts of what heroes and criminals do (kill, beat, evade, rescue, solve) when no such role label or genre marker is present.

1161841.title: "And" joining two nouns or names
1161841.explanation: Fires on the linking word itself when it joins two things, people or names into a pair or list: "between us and the Apaches", "his parents and sister's deaths", "oil and natural gas", "Robarts, Lubbock, and Co.", "Batman and his partner", "Joker and Harley", "Gus and Ralph". It fires the same way on other spellings and languages of that word: dialect "un'" and "an'", Chinese 與 and 和, old Portuguese "he", and occasionally "or", a slash or a list comma; it even fires on the letters "eland" inside a surname. It does not fire on "and" inside a measurement or count ("two minutes and 52 seconds", "17 years and 325 days") or between two verbs ("debuted and peaked", "find and kill"), which belong to the opposite pole.

1176854.title: The word "superhero" and its variants
1176854.explanation: Fires on the word "superhero" itself and its close variants: "superheroes", "super hero", "Super Hero" in titles (Marvel Super Hero Island, Super Hero Squad Show, Superhero Sundays), "superheroics", the "superv" of "supervillain", and "Hero" in the superhero anime title My Hero Academia. It is mostly a reaction to the marked token, strongest when the word labels a genre or a kind of character near the start of a text ("a superhero webcomic", "the superhero team", "a monkey superhero"). It fires only weakly on superhero-story text that lacks the word (Gotham, Batman at the opening of a summary), and plain "hero" or "super" in non-superhero senses is not among the strong firings.

1290289.title: Linking word before a counted group of things
1290289.explanation: The unit fires on a small mid-phrase token that sits between a quantity word and the plural thing it counts: "98% of [44 critics]", "most of [the island's population]", "All of [the remaining DJs]", "many other [people]", "two new [animals]", "both Philadelphia [teams]", "because all [emotions]", "join the [two rings]", "using [different circles]". It reacts to the position (a set, share or number of items is about to be named), not to one particular word, and the peak token varies (of, all, other, new, the, using, a digit). A second, looser group is source code, where it fires in the middle of an expression that reaches into a collection or variable (arguments["..."], .namespaces.all, d[s], "is not None"); the link to the first group is weak, and the plot-summary firings are faint and mixed, so this is only a partial pattern.

1295861.title: Linking "to" after trying, deciding, telling verbs
1295861.explanation: It fires in the middle of a plot-summary sentence on a small connecting word, most often "to", right after a verb of attempting, deciding, asking or disclosing: "tries to", "decide to", "unable to", "one hour to", "does not reveal what she overheard to Dan", "reveals his identity to Gordon", "divulge the alibi to Callahan". Many of the sentences are about one character telling, hiding or revealing something to another (a secret, an identity, an alibi), and the unit peaks at the point where the action or the listener is about to be named. The pattern is loose: other peaks fall on "and", "who", "they", "been", "the", a line break in a review and a field name in Go code, so it is more a mid-clause grammatical position than a single topic. It does not fire on sentence openings or on the content words themselves.

1340707.title: Writer's passing verdict: "a bold move", "unusual for"
1340707.explanation: It fires where the writer steps back and passes a judgement on what was just stated, peaking on the judging adjective or on the generic noun that completes the phrase: "a bold move, considering", "a curious position for the grandson", "an unusual task for female officials", "a tough name for a girl", "impressive figure for those times", "Odd. Very odd.", "Unnecessary check, probably". The trigger is the meaning of the construction, a rating of something against a norm or expectation (unusual, uncommon, difficult, reasonable, important, relatively young), usually just before a qualifier such as "for ...", "considering ...", "when compared to ..." or "to ..."; it is not tied to one word. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on set-off state adjectives that characterise a person or thing (jealous, suspicious, traumatized, unauthorized, different, possible). Ordinary adjectives that simply describe an object inside a narrative, with no such stepping-back assessment, do not set it off.

1341224.title: Linking word before naming a known place or person
1341224.explanation: The unit fires on a linking word at the point where the sentence is about to name a place, team or person that is already established or easy to guess: "returns to" (Rome), "make it to" (New York), "campus" (of Boston College), "presence" (in Spain), "represented" (India), "win" (over Australia / in Pittsburgh), "loss" (in San Jose), "from" (Tom), "thinking" (that Tom), "granting" (Daniel), "assisting" (the Nazis), "overhears" (Fiona). The marked token itself varies widely (a preposition, a verb, a comma, or a noun such as win, loss, presence, campus), so the unit is reacting to what comes next, not to a particular word. It is a loose pattern: the same words do not fire when no specific named complement is expected, and a few peaks ("adjunct", "Française", "identity", "death") fit only weakly.

1405944.title: Clause subject just before its verb
1405944.explanation: This is a grammar unit, not a topic unit. It fires on the last word of a clause's subject, at the moment a finite verb is due next, most often a short pronoun (I, we, she, they, you, it, that) that follows a linking word or clause opener such as "but", "that", "when", "if ..., ", "so" or a colon: "but I was wrong", "said that they were no longer able", "I'm not even mad, that's amazing", "when I'm at home", "penalties that she had ignored". It also fires at the end of a longer subject ("the ellipsoidal constraint holds", "The life with which you are familiar is", "An attorney for Cowles argued"), and the next word is usually an auxiliary or a form of "be" (was, were, 're, 'm, 's, had, needn't). The same pronouns as objects or after the verb do not fire it, and the subject matter of the passage (school story, physics, cooking review, code comment) does not matter; in the plot summaries it is weak.

1440851.title: Japanese tokusatsu heroes and assumed hero identities
1440851.explanation: The unit fires most strongly inside texts about Japanese costumed, transforming superhero series (Kamen Rider / Masked Rider, Ultraman, Super Sentai, Metal Hero, Garo, Zebraman), peaking on pieces of the hero or series names ("Kamen", "Rider", "Den-O", "Dekarangers") and on other tokens once that context is established, including dates and character names. A weaker, related group is a person taking on or holding a superhero persona: "Krishna as Krrish", "Ultraman Dyna's human alter ego", "save Gotham as Batman", "take up the mantle of", "reveals his identity", "his role as vigilante". Ordinary cartoons, Western animation and non-hero Japanese or anime material do not trigger it, and the peak token itself is not a fixed word; what matters is the transforming-hero context.

1444956.title: Linking word just before a villain is named
1444956.explanation: The unit fires in superhero, comic-book and fantasy plot text on the linking word (a preposition or verb such as in, with, for, from, by, to, named, stop, infiltrate, allow, fulfill) that comes right before the name of an antagonist: a villain, an evil ruler, or an enemy organization. Examples are "mole in [Black Manta's organization]", "infiltrate [Shadowspire]", "save Xandar from [Ronan the Accuser]", "sided with [Rita Repulsa]", "reports to [Deathstroke]", "attempting to stop [the evil Skeletor]", "alliance with [Two-Face]", "stop [the Joker]". It is reacting to what is about to come next, the villain or enemy faction the sentence is leading up to, not to the marked word itself. The same connecting words before or after a hero's name (for example "Spider-Man and") do not fire it, and it is weaker when the upcoming thing is a place or object tied to the villain (Lord Farquaad of Duloc, the Lazarus Pit).

1461365.title: Mid-statement code tokens reusing earlier-defined names
1461365.explanation: Fires almost only inside source code (Python, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, C), part-way through a statement, on an identifier or operator at the point where the line re-uses something set up a few lines earlier: a helper or variable just defined (_prt, _dict, Info, objects, hash512_modq, return_value) or a formula term that repeats the line before ($C *, $saturation *, (*Q).front, && between the two halves of a range test). It reacts to the position in the code and to what predictably comes next, not to any particular word; the peak tokens are all different, and none of the top peaks sits on a definition, a comment or a docstring. The few prose hits are weaker and only loosely similar (a fixed phrase 'hand to hand', 'the precise time he said he would leave'), and the plot-summary sentences (0.3 to 0.6, on tells, fighting, kills, battle) show no clear pattern of their own.

1463527.title: Middle piece of a long or compound word
1463527.explanation: The unit fires on a word piece in the middle of a long, multi-piece word or name, after its opening and before its ending: Cin-emat-heque / Cinem-ate-ca / синем-ат-ека / Cin-emat-ography, несем-ит-ские (non-Semitic), pré-h-ist-órico, ne-oph-yte, Galá-ct-ico, Franç-afrique, super-c-rim-inals, war-t-orn, outer-most. It reacts to the token's position inside an unfinished word, often a prefixed or foreign-language word (Russian, Portuguese, Spanish, Tagalog) or a quoted label or name for a group or place ("scum", «secta de Mahoma», "Little Tokyo", Criminal Investigation Division), rather than to any one meaning. There is no single topic: the cinema/cinematheque words, the Franc- words and the crim- words recur, but the rest are unrelated, and complete short words or ordinary word endings do not fire it.

1464129.title: Word just before an expected "change"
1464129.explanation: The unit seems to fire in anticipation of the next word rather than on the marked token itself. The clearest group peaks on the word immediately before 'change', 'changes' or 'reform': 'positive' (four times), 'dislike', 'make', 'radical social (reform)', and close relatives where something new or altered is coming ('a large price increase', 'welcoming to new experiences', 'ready for his fresh perspective', '= new' in code after a ChangeListener name). A second, looser group is small linking words inside fixed names and phrases where the continuation is predictable: 'Programme for International', '1s and 2s', 'study in detail', and in the plot summaries 'League of Shadows/Assassins', 'Fortress of Solitude', 'fear of bats'. It does not fire on the word 'change' itself, and the two groups do not reduce cleanly to one idea.

1480716.title: Organisation names: intelligence services, WikiLeaks, "Service" identifiers
1480716.explanation: No single clean idea. The strongest firings land on the first word of a formal organisation name or title in text about state secrecy, surveillance and online information: "National" just before "Intelligence Service" (the South Korean NIS, three times), "WikiLeaks", "International" before "Service for Human Rights", "Executive" before "Director of the Wikimedia Foundation". A second group is Java code, where it fires on "Service" in "ServiceLoader" and on unrelated tokens at the start of a statement or annotation. It does not fire on the word "service" or "national" in general, and in the plot summaries its firings are weak and scattered ("via", "Watergate", "some", "animosity"), so the link to spy agencies and leak organisations is only a loose tendency.

1482139.title: Partway into a specific name or term
1482139.explanation: The unit fires on a token after which the rest of a specific name or fixed term is due: the first part of a product, brand or proper name (DS«i» XL, DS«i»Ware, «Wii» Remote, Dol«by» Pro Logic, «Dynamic» Flash, «AVC» MOV, «Team» Magma, «Pokémon» Trainer, D«ach»au, D«wayne» Peel, «match»-needle, «Berlin»-based). More weakly it fires on a linking word that is about to introduce a particular place, person or thing ("to", "from", "of", "named", "by", "with", Chinese 由 and 區), which is all that shows up in the plot summaries. Many of the strongest cases are consumer-electronics and video-game names (Nintendo, Lumia, Canon), but the pattern is loose and looks like anticipation of the next part of a name rather than one topic; ordinary words in running prose with no name or term coming do not fire.

1483154.title: Just before naming a superhero-story figure
1483154.explanation: The unit fires in superhero and comic-book film plots (Iron Man, Captain America, Blade, Green Lantern, Fantastic Four, Nick Fury) on the word just before a specific known name from that story world is due.
