Most often the peak is a role or rank word placed in front of a person's name, usually someone in charge or a close relation: "S.H.I.E.L.D. director" (Nick Fury), "leader" (Raza), "mentor" (Whistler), "supervisor", "boss", "President", "Lord", "father"; a second group is a linking word such as "by", "of" or "for" right before such a name or organisation ("led by" Ra's al Ghul, "owned by" Deacon Frost, "codes for" Stark Industries). It is about what comes next rather than the word itself: the same role words in ordinary films or non-fiction, or when no franchise name is about to follow, are not among its strong firings, and a few weaker peaks ("secret", "fulfill", "a", "the") fit only loosely.

1485188.title: Crime-drama franchise characters: role and office links
1485188.explanation: It fires in text about serious crime, police and detective franchises (NCIS above all, also CSI, Castle, Gotham, Detective Comics, the detective Dakota North) and about the Gordon family and other law-enforcement figures in Batman stories. The peak sits on the small linking word or title that ties a named character to a rank, office, agency or identity: "daughter of [police commissioner James Gordon]", "commander of [NERV]", "promoted to [commissioner]", "taking on the mantle of [Batgirl]", "the former [Batgirl]", "district attorney", cast-list "as" before a police character, and "back to" headquarters or DC. A weaker second group is articles on Japanese anime franchises (Evangelion, Gundam, Ouran). It does not respond to cartoon comedy (Looney Tunes, Family Guy), nor to the same words "of", "to", "as" in ordinary plots with no police, detective or crime-franchise setting.

1485789.title: Slot just before a named character or warlord
1485789.explanation: The unit fires on the small linking word or title that comes right before the name of a well-known figure from an established cast is due: "surrender to", "allied forces of", "close aide of", "shot several times by", "alias used by", "the warlord", "Wei general", or a comma inside a list of names. It is strongest in articles about late Han and Three Kingdoms China, where the next words are Cao Cao, Liu Bei or Cao Pi, and second strongest in comic-book articles, where the next words are a character such as the Punisher, Lois Lane or Flash Thompson; in the plot summaries it fires the same way on "adopt", "kidnaps", "abducts", "mastermind" and "the main character is" just before a character is named. It reacts to what is about to come, not to the marked word itself: the same "of", "to" or "by" before an ordinary noun, a place or a date does not fire it, and neither does text about comics publishers and creators rather than the characters.

1487126.title: Slot just before a screen character's name
1487126.explanation: Fires on the word that comes right before a fictional character is named, mostly in text about television series and comic-book adaptations (Riverdale, Gotham, Arrow, Titans, The Flash). The strongest cases are cast-list and career wording such as "Erin Richards as", "Arrow as", "played", "portrayed primarily by", and role labels that lead into a name ("police commissioner", "wealthy industrialist", "criminal psychologist", "childhood friend", "Their leader,"). It is reacting to what comes next (a character name, sometimes a show title after "sitcom" or "TV series"), not to the marked word itself; a few weaker hits on the "1" of 2019 / COVID-19 in TV production sections do not fit. Ordinary uses of "as" or "and" outside a casting or character-introduction context do not fire it.

1500498.title: 2010s US network TV shows, especially Arrowverse
1500498.explanation: Fires in encyclopedia-style text about American network television series of roughly 2012 to 2018, most strongly the DC Comics adaptations on The CW (The Flash, Arrow, Supergirl, Legends of Tomorrow, 'the Arrowverse') and secondarily CBS-era shows such as The Big Bang Theory, CSI, The Mentalist, Castle and The King of Queens. The peak sits on a small linking token just before or inside the show, network or date being named ('The' before Flash or CW, 'the' before Arrowverse, 'on' before CBS, 'Theory', the '2' of 2012, 'starring'), so it reacts to the surrounding context and to what is about to be named, not to the token itself. In plot summaries it fires more weakly on linking words ('of', 'by', 'to', ',') in Batman and other DC stories just before a named DC character or place. Ordinary uses of 'the', 'on' or a year outside this television and DC setting do not fire it.

1502596.title: Title before a hero's supporting-cast name
1502596.explanation: The clearest group is a rank, job or relation word placed right before the name of an established supporting figure in a superhero or detective story, mostly police and other authority figures: "Commissioner" (Gordon, Loeb), district "attorney" (Harvey Dent), "supervisor" and "boss" (Perry White), "reporters" (Vicki Vale), "led by" (Gordon), "her father" (commissioner Gordon), and "as" before Martha Rodgers in a cast list. The unit fires on the title word, before the name itself, and not on the hero's or the villains' names. A second group is romanised Japanese names and words, especially ones beginning Oto-/Ota- (O«to»ya, «Ot»oko, «Ot»oboke, O«TO»-NANO, «ot»aku) and the recurring cast of Detective Conan (inspector «Meg»ure, «Son»oko, Kait«ou» Kid); this looks partly like a spelling response and is only loosely tied to the first group.

1504750.title: Link word just before an asylum or institution name
1504750.explanation: The unit fires on a small token that sits one step before a fixed, highly predictable continuation, and it is reacting to what comes next rather than to the marked word. The strongest and most consistent group is a linking word ("of", "at", "to") or modifier right before the name of a psychiatric or medical institution: "patients of / at / taken to / incarcerated at [Arkham Asylum]", "committed to [an asylum]", "American Board of [Psychiatry]", "Behavioural [Psychotherapy]", "Westside [Medical Center]", "spinal [cord]", plus the first name "Nora" before "Fries". A second, looser group is the middle of a number or name whose rest is fixed: the second digit of a year (1«8»32, 19«0»5), the dash in a date range or ISBN, and "Sh" in Shlomo/Shmuel. It does not peak on the institution name itself, and the year-digit cases are weak evidence because the opposite pole fires on them too.

1512347.title: Linking word just before an expected proper name
1512347.explanation: The unit fires on a small connecting token (of, by, on, to, for, against, the, a comma, 'while', 'god', the Chinese verb for 'acquired', or the middle of a model number) at the point where the context makes a specific proper name the obvious next thing: 'Third Dynasty of' before Ur, 'New Gods of' before Apokolips, 'based on' before Symbian OS, 'Intel,' before AMD, 'by' before Calculator, 'League of' before Shadows. It is reacting to what comes next, not to the marked word itself. The strongest cases fall into three related groups: handheld devices and their makers (Sony CLIÉ, Palm, Motorola, model codes such as PEG-TJ27 and N710), DC Comics characters, teams and places, and ancient Mesopotamian places. The same linking words in ordinary prose, where no particular named company, faction, character or place is due next, do not fire it, and the opposite pole takes 'using'/'in' before the name of a programming tool.

1514566.title: Linking word just before a named place
1514566.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking word, most often a preposition (at, of, into, onto, to, with) and sometimes a comma, dash, 'North' or a verb like 'destroy' or 'investigate', at the point where the next words will name a specific place, venue, institution or other particular thing: 'a race at [Hard Rock Stadium]', 'construction of [Interstate 66]', 'the island of [Delos]', 'break into [Axis Chemicals]', 'lures her to [the Flugelheim Museum]'. It is anticipating what comes next rather than reacting to the marked word or to a topic, and it appears mostly in factual, encyclopedic or plot-summary prose about sports, roads, ships and locations. The same prepositions before a body part or a held object ('in his arms', 'in one hand', 'upon his shoulder') do not fire it; those belong to the opposite pole.

1516685.title: Slot just before a specific name is given
1516685.explanation: The unit fires on the word or mark that introduces a specific proper name that is about to come, not on the name itself: a role or descriptor noun in apposition ("the deranged actor" Basil Karlo, "the female deity" Atropos, "blackface entertainer" Tom Baron, "the veteran assassin" Deathstroke, "the shapeshifter" Clayface, "Black Glove member" Le Bossu, "another mobster named" Salvatore Valestra), the opening bracket before an actor's name in a cast-style plot summary ("Ting-pong's mother (" Lee Heung-kam), an opening quote or "entitled" before a work's title, or a linking word such as "was", "by", "for" right before the person is named. A smaller related group is the slot just before a specific identifying detail of appearance, mainly a colour of hair or skin ("emerald-green hair", "dyed his hair green", a cat's yellow glow in a Chinese passage). It reacts to what is about to come next; a role word used generically with no name following ("an actor", "a member") and the names themselves are not where it peaks.

1520757.title: Just before a named team, gang or character
1520757.explanation: This unit fires on what is about to come: it peaks on the small linking word (of, the, by, in, to, into, at, a slash, an opening quote mark) or on a name-starting piece ("Super", "Jack") right before a specific proper name is spelled out. The name is most often a team, gang, organisation or costumed character in DC superhero text: "a horde of [Parademons]", "a member of [the Black Lantern Corps]", "killed by Super[boy-Prime]", "the Foot Clan and the [League of Assassins]", "a gang called "[the Mutants]", "mutated into [Poison Ivy]". Weaker cases do the same before named organisations outside comics (the Los Angeles crime family, the Church of Satan, a wrestling promotion, GM Super Turbine). The same linking words before ordinary common nouns, or after the name has already been given, do not set it off.

1528083.title: Slot before a named superhero-universe character
1528083.explanation: The unit fires in text about comic-book superhero worlds, mostly Marvel (X-Men, S.H.I.E.L.D., Spider-Man, Iron Man, Captain America, Wolverine), on the word just before a named character or organisation of that world is about to be given. The marked token is not the name but the lead-in to it: a role word (director, assistant, scientist, Agent, liaison, father, friend) or a connective (of, to, under, as, plays, a dash or an opening bracket in a cast list), followed by Nick Fury, Stryker, Felicia Hardy, Pepper Potts, the Essex Corporation and so on. So it is reacting to what comes next rather than to the word itself; a few weaker peaks (marries, recalls, kidnapped, meeting) are verbs that lead up to a named person. The same role words and connectives outside superhero stories, or before a place or an event rather than a character, do not seem to fire it.

1536542.title: Superhero-comics text, at a specific franchise name
1536542.explanation: The unit fires inside text about superhero comic books and their adaptations (DC, Marvel, Watchmen), and peaks where a specific name from that world is being spelled out or is about to be given: comic creators (Tom Lyle, Joe Kubert, 'by' Mike Mignola, 'illustrator:' Dave Gibbons), characters and places with odd spellings (Sl-ade, Z-od, Z-sasz, Z-enn-La, Dev-Em, Sch-midlapp), and dotted agency acronyms (S.H.I.E.L.D., S.T.A.R. Labs). It reacts to the surrounding comic-book setting more than to any one word, so the marked tokens vary (a first name fragment, a full stop inside an acronym, 'secret', 'super'). General talk about superheroes or about having or lacking superpowers, with no particular name being produced, does not fire it (that is the opposite pole), and the same name fragments outside a comics setting should not either.

1537827.title: Word-start "av" (avowed, avenged); pre-name list slots
1537827.explanation: No single idea covers all the passages; there are two groups. The largest and clearest (half of the top passages) is the word fragment " av" at the start of a verb in older English prose, just before it is completed as avowed, avenged, availed or avengest; here the unit reacts to the marked fragment and the ending it expects. The second, looser group is a position just before a specific name is supplied, usually in a list of creatures or characters: " P"/" p" before -teranodon and -terosaurs, "included" before a list of Ice Age animals, "2." before "Polar bears", "ticker symbol" before "HEAR", and in the plot summaries the commas and small words ("from", "to", "befriending", "Cob-ble") inside or just before lists of named villains. It fires only weakly in the plot summaries, and ordinary commas in lists of company or brand names belong to the opposite pole, so it is not a general list-comma unit.

1543765.title: Slot just before a character's name is given
1543765.explanation: The unit fires at the point where the text is about to name a person or character, usually a supporting figure being brought into a story or cast list: after a relation or role word ("Bruce's girlfriend", "Batman's ally", "the dead man's niece,", "psychologist and lawyer", "Police Commissioner", "Sir"), after a linking word that calls for a name ("meets", "is dating", "meet with", "led by", "role as", "Sean Pertwee as", "including"), or on the comma or full stop after which a new named character opens the clause. It reacts to what is coming next, not to the marked token itself, which varies from commas to verbs to nouns. It is commonest in plot summaries and articles about fiction (many of them DC comics, also Arthurian and film plots); the same words where no name is due to follow do not show up among its passages.

1546344.title: Linking token inside name-dense lists, before next name
1546344.explanation: There is no single meaning here; the unit fires on small connecting tokens rather than on content. The clearest group is cast and character lists, especially in Telugu film articles and plots, where it peaks on the comma, "and", "as" or opening bracket that comes right after one person's name and just before the next name ("N. T. Rama Rao Jr.,", "Mangamma (", "Sathya (", "Tanikella Bharani and", "Lesley-Ann Brandt as", "Ren and"). A second group is "of" after a noun that is about to be completed by a specific named thing ("the introduction of" Bantu Education, "a committee of" correspondence, "a vat of", "overrun by"), and a third is fragments in the middle of long or foreign words ("super-fl-uous", "simb-ol-os", a Greek word, "R-idd-ler", "May-or"). What these share is only position: a join in the middle of a phrase where a specific name or term is expected next; the same words in plain running prose with no name or list around them do not fire it.

1548330.title: Just before a specific title, issue or name
1548330.explanation: The unit fires at the point where the text is about to supply a particular proper name or identifier, so it reacts to what comes next more than to the marked word. The clearest group is comic-book citations: "DC" just before Comics or Ink, and "Batman" or "in" just before a series title and issue number (Batman #500, Batman: Vengeance of Bane #1, in Tales of the Teen Titans #44). A second group is American college sport, just before a conference, championship or team name (the Northeast Conference, ECAC North Championships, LIU Sharks, "made up of" a list of colleges), and a few weaker cases are other slots awaiting a name or number (Senator ..., company ..., a colon before named people, a year). It does not fire when Batman is simply a character acting in the story; the word has to be opening a publication title or similar named item.

1552347.title: Just before an expected name: butler then Alfred
1552347.explanation: In the plot summaries the pattern is tight: it fires on "butler" (or "caretaker", or the comma right after) in phrases like "Bruce's butler, Alfred Pennyworth", and on "a scuffle with" at Wayne Manor, that is, at the slot just before the name Alfred Pennyworth is due. The reference-corpus passages are much more mixed and weaker, but most share the same position: a small token right before a strongly predictable completion, such as "Edward and" / "Alice and" before Bella, "Krist-in" before Scott Thomas, "diagnosed with" / "she has" before cancer or leukemia, "invitation from" before his nephew, the first digit of a year ("1" before 986, 900, 953), or the middle of a Polish or Czech word. It reacts to what is about to come rather than to the marked token itself; it does not fire on the name Alfred once it has been written, and ordinary uses of "and", "with" or a comma with no obvious continuation do not trigger it. Outside the butler case I could not find one clean idea.

1553950.title: Start of a comic-book character's or place's name
1553950.explanation: Fires on the first token of the proper name of a known comic-book-universe character or place, in text about Marvel or DC stories: the given name of a civilian or supporting character (Steve Rogers, Steve Trevor, Carol Ferris, Mark Richards, Victor Fries, Rachel Dawes, Simon Hurt, Jack Drake, Barbara Wilson) or the opening piece of an invented name (Krakoa, Kraven, Krystalin, Klarion, Utopia, N'astirh, Elasti-Girl, Kiersey). It reacts at the moment the name begins, when the surrounding superhero story has made clear which entity is being named and the rest of the name is predictable. It does not fire on the headline hero names (Batman, Captain America) or on general talk about superheroes and comics, which is what the opposite pole picks up, and nothing here shows the same first names firing outside a comic-book setting.

1557081.title: First name Robert; function words before expected terms
1557081.explanation: There is no single clean idea here; the passages fall into two loose groups. The clearest is the first name 'Robert' at the point where a surname is due (Robert Mitchum in cast brackets, Robert Emmet, Robert Louis Stevenson, Robert Maverick), with weaker firings on other name beginnings (Ed-mure, Bruce, Des-i). The second is small function words in physics, mathematics and source-code text (the, of, by, is, in, two, import, a digit in a variable name) just before a term that the earlier text makes predictable, such as 'the magnitude of the [angular momentum]' or 'the number of [different output values]'. At most the groups share that the next word is strongly expected; the firings in the plot summaries are weak (under half strength) and scattered, and the same words elsewhere do not reliably fire it.

1560401.title: Slot just before a specific name is supplied
1560401.explanation: Fires on the word or punctuation mark that opens a slot about to be filled with a particular proper name, so it reacts to what comes next rather than to the marked token. The clearest and strongest case is "under" after a degree and year in a scholar's biography ("Ph.D. in 1975 under [the supervision of X]"); the same shape appears in "winners; [names]", "family, [Procellariidae]", "founded by Don Morris and [second founder]", "killed by Baby [Face Nelson]", "2015: The [film title]", and in plots on a role noun just before the person is named ("young son [Bruce]", "psychiatrist [Hugo Strange]", "his friend, [officer Rod Williams]", "found by [officer John Blake]"). Outside the "under the supervision of" group the firings are weaker and more scattered (a few land on the first digit of a year or mid-name), so the pattern is loose, and ordinary uses of "under", "by" or "and" that do not lead into a name are not shown to fire it.

1561173.title: About to name a DC supporting character
1561173.explanation: In texts about DC superhero stories, above all Wonder Woman, Arrow, the Flash and Batman, the unit fires on the word just before a supporting character is named: a linking word or verb ("from" Sir Patrick, "hires" one of his students, "to" Wonder Woman, "with" Oliver Queen, "as" Detective Quentin Lance, "including" Black Canary), a comma inside a list of cast names, or a job or family label ("reporter" Lois Lane, "psychiatrist" Hugo Strange, "archivist" Lucius Fox, antiquities "dealer" Diana Prince, his "wife" Martha). It reacts to what comes next in that setting, not to the marked word itself; a few weaker cases are outside DC but have the same shape ("chooses" Lancelot, a rival "of" Stanton and Anthony). Superman and Krypton comics text before a villain or creator name does not fire it; that is the opposite pole.

1580619.title: Linking word before superhero-universe place or group
1580619.explanation: Fires inside Marvel and DC superhero plots and character pages on a small linking word (in, of, at, from, by, upon, 's) that opens a phrase naming a place, facility, team or agency of that fictional world: "S.H.I.E.L.D.'s" (Helicarrier), "at the" Flash Museum, "in" S.T.A.R. Labs, "of" the Birds of Prey / the Outsiders, "at" Pleasant Hill, "from" a D.O.D.C. truck, "from Wayne" Manor, "Ace Chemicals". It depends on the superhero setting built up by the text before it and on the coming location or organisation, not on the particular preposition; the same prepositions in ordinary films or non-superhero articles are not among its strong passages. The pattern is loose: some hits ("in order to", "age of miracles", "time travels to 2023", "Criminal mastermind") are only superhero-context linking words without a place or group following.

1581948.title: Blank space just before a number in digits
1581948.explanation: The unit fires on the blank space token that sits directly in front of a number written in digits, so it is reacting to what comes next: a numeral is about to be written. The numbers are of every kind: licence plates and room, apartment or street numbers (TLH 858, TIU 250, apartment 1303, room 305, 1005 Edgewater Drive), counts and durations (30,000 cavalry, 14 championships, 10 minutes, 20 minutes), ranks and days (9th greatest, 17th top, May 10, 9th of September) and years used as labels (1991 Local Government Code, 2008 financial crisis, ordinance of 1970); in the plot summaries it is the same space before ages, scores and years (16-year-old, 179, 1955, 1929, 1999). It does not fire on the digits themselves, on numbers spelled out in words, or on ordinary spaces between words. The opposite pole of the same neuron also sits on some spaces before numbers, and the passages do not make clear what separates the two.

1587002.title: Mid-phrase token just before a proper name
1587002.explanation: The unit fires on a token that opens or sits inside a naming phrase, at the point where the rest of a specific name is due next. The clearest cases are a first name before its surname (Rachel Roth, David Phelps, Jordan Pryce, Rachael Lampa, Jean-Paul), a title or kinship word before the person's name (councilman Arthur Reeves, Attorney Harvey Dent, Mayor Krol, daughter Talia, case worker Tracy), and a preposition before a named place (under / at Wayne Manor); the person is usually a secondary figure being introduced in a plot, cast list or credit. A looser group of peaks falls on ordinary words in the middle of a phrase (about, tells, one, neural, inter, of, a digit of a year), so the pattern is only partly one idea. It does not fire on the last token of a completed name or on the main character's name repeated later.

1588941.title: Completing token of a game or franchise title
1588941.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes the proper name of an entertainment product or franchise, most strongly video-game titles and their sequel markers at the start of an article: "Crackdown 2", "Bad Company 2", "Dungeon Siege II", "Grand Theft Auto IV", "Octo Expansion", "Super Kirby Clash", "Lego Brawls", "Infamous Second Son". It also fires on other pop-culture brand names as they are completed: "Shazam", "Golden Globes", "BlackBerry 10", "WWE 24/7 Championship", "Millennium Falcon", "King Kong", "Arkham Knight", "Arkham City", "Batman", "DC", "Nygma", "Hamill". It reacts to the marked token as part of a recognised title; ordinary numbers, Roman numerals or common words outside a game, comic, film or brand name do not trigger it.

1612452.title: First letter (mostly A) of a split word
1612452.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a one- or two-character piece that begins a longer word the model has to finish, most often the letter A. The strongest cases are "A" opening Ainsworth, Auschwitz, Aika, Apathy and APL, the Cyrillic "а" opening the Russian words for amphitheatres, airports and Assyria, and French or Spanish "a" in l'aile and aledaños; a smaller group has G or a "ga" sound instead (Glastonbury, slow-grown, GCPD, Korean "ga" in Covent Garden, Japanese "ga" in Gundam). It works across languages and scripts, so it is about the word-opening fragment, not the meaning of the passage. It is not every initial letter: one-letter starts of place names after a hyphen (Hamburg-Aarhus, Köln-Aachen) go to the opposite pole, and the firings in the plot summaries are weak and only loosely related ("A" logo, Baltimore, small words before "asylum" or "Arkham").

1618229.title: Word piece starting with b inside a compound
1618229.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a word fragment beginning with the letter b, most often "-b" straight after a hyphen, at the point where the rest of the compound is easy to guess (anti-bullying, carbon-burning, thallium-boron, water-borne, semi-basement, also "Bio" in Bioinformatics, "b" in bivalent, "B" in Bane and Batcycle, and the Arabic prefix letter b). The strongest and most repeated case is "anti-b" before "ullying". Weaker firings are other mid-term fragments inside technical compounds (carbon monoxide, metal-oxide-semiconductor, Mycobacterium, Strain, Iron & Steel), so it is partly a general 'in the middle of a compound term' signal. It is about spelling and word-joining, not about bullying, chemistry or any topic, and whole ordinary words starting with b in running prose do not appear.

1620110.title: Split-off "B" or "New" starting New York names
1620110.explanation: The unit fires on the first fragment of a name whose ending is still to come, above all a split-off capital "B" (also "-B", "/B") or the word "New", in text about New York and its region: B|inghamton, B|rooklyn, B|roadway, B|MT, B|ergen County, New| York, St|uyvesant, and the same in Korean (뉴|욕) and Russian (Б|ингемтонского). It is anticipating the rest of the name rather than reacting to what has been said, so it also fires on other broken B-words with no New York link (B|urt Wonderstone, B|orman Brothers, B|altimore, dark-b|rown). Names written as whole words in the same passages (Brooklyn Bridge, Buffalo, Manhattan) are not the peaks. In the plot summaries the firings are weaker and looser, mostly on a word just before a person is named (by, with, finds, approaches, killing) and once on the B of Bane.

1633237.title: Just before "funding" in prose; before x-index in code
1633237.explanation: The strongest firings fall into two groups that share only a next-word-prediction character. In prose (English and Arabic) it fires on the word just before money granted to a project or body is named: "get more [funding]", "lack of [funding]", "reduced [funding]", "their [funding] will be cut off", "secure nearly $100 million", "increase in state appropriations", "find that crucial investment", so it reacts to a context where funding, financing or investment is about to be mentioned, not to the marked word itself. In source code it fires on a name just before it is indexed or called with a variable beginning with x (opts.options[x], grid[x][y], col_type_dict[x], np.amin(xst), range(xstart). Ordinary talk of money, prices or pay that is not about securing or cutting funding, and code indexing with other variables, do not appear; the plot-summary firings (pull funding, secured $500,000, demanding approval) are weak echoes of the funding group.

1643584.title: Unexpected token straight after a number or code
1643584.explanation: This first-layer unit reacts to the marked token in its immediate setting: most peaks are the token that comes directly after a digit or a code ending in a digit, when that token is an unusual follower, such as ' Stops' after bus route codes K9, F8 and P12, ' Neighbor' after 2018, ' sworn' after 7,100, ' demol' after 9,398, ' incentive' after 2010, or glued-on fragments like '(or', '-most', 'incl' and '/network'. It also fires on the odd low-quote character '‚' used as a comma inside or after a number (4‚861, 1958‚). A few strong peaks do not follow a digit at all (the name piece 'lland', '……' after a symbol, '。(' in Chinese text), so it is partly a loose set of rare tokens and unusual punctuation rather than one clean idea. Ordinary followers of numbers, such as a normal comma, do not appear among the strongest passages, and it is weak in the plot summaries (kilometers after 142, percent after 40, and unrelated names).

1648203.title: Tokens with a quote mark fused to a character
1648203.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a single token in which an apostrophe or single quote is glued to one more character, such as '^ at the start of a regex string, (', inside implode(', ', ...), 's opening a quoted key like 'status' or 'secret', ';, '- or 'D. It is strongest in PHP and Python source code where a string literal opens or closes, and it also fires on 's and 'd in ordinary words (bash's, Shopify's, terr'd), but only weakly (about a third of maximum) on the possessive 's in plain prose such as plot summaries. It does not fire on variable-interpolation tokens such as {$ or ${, which belong to the opposite pole, and it is not about what the surrounding text means.

1651724.title: Word piece "sburg" in town names; rare characters
1651724.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself, not to meaning: most of its English firings are on the word piece "sburg" that finishes a town name after a first piece such as Pitt, Warren, Aug or Schuckmann (Pittsburg, The Pittsburg Press, Warrensburg, Augsburg, Schuckmannsburg). Its very strongest firings are a second, unrelated group of uncommon Chinese characters (硭 in the mineral name 硭硝 and in an instrument name, 膊 in 肩膊 "shoulder", 羊毛 "fleece") plus one Korean word, 예수 (Jesus). Names ending in -burg that are spelt with other pieces in the same passages (Gettysburg, Fredericksburg, Chambersburg, Pittsburgh written whole) are not the peaks. The plot-summary firings are weak (everlasting, Batman, borne, unwitting) and show no pattern.

1652692.title: Spaced dash separating dates, codes or datelines
1652692.explanation: Fires on a dash token that has a space before it and acts as a separator: the em dash between birth and death dates (December 25, 1908 — February 20, 1993), after a news dateline (TAMPA —), after a code or abbreviation in a list or legend (VA-34 —, QF —), and the plain or double hyphen in year ranges and code comments (2016 - 2018, codefragments.py --, -f --strip-all). It is a reaction to the token itself, strongest near the start of a document right after a number, date or capitalised label; a few odd peaks sit in the same slot after a number or abbreviation (Pepsi after 1988, Japanese 以外, Korean 이후 meaning 'other than'/'since'). An em dash without a space inside a sentence fires only weakly, and a tight hyphen inside a designation such as M-1 or MQ-28 belongs to the opposite pole.

1653096.title: First word right after a number
1653096.explanation: The unit fires on the token that comes immediately after a string of digits: a name or noun following a year or figure ("2016 Autodesk", "460 Northwestern", "1998 Northwestern", "2001 WWE", "1947 Harvard", "2020 Ontario", "1,000 Subway", "559,867 admissions", "2019, crowdfunding"), the Korean counter "경" (of 경기, games) after "100", "110", "967", the Japanese "となっている" after a postcode, and URL or code pieces after digits ("100&utm", "169.254.169.254/latest", "2001/XMLSchema"). What the word means does not matter; what matters is that a number has just ended and ordinary text or a name resumes. The same words elsewhere, without a number directly before them, give little or nothing: the plot-summary firings are weak (0.35 at most) and only partly fit ("$80,000 ransom", "2004 Henley", "105 Freeway").

1656275.title: The word "signal"
1656275.explanation: Fires on the token "signal" itself (also "Signal" and "signals"), whatever the sense: a radio or Morse signal, signal processing, signal transduction in cells, an honest signal in animal behaviour, a railway signal-box, the place name Signal Hill, the Python module in "import signal", or the verb "to signal relevance". It reacts to the word, not to the surrounding meaning, so texts about messages, broadcasts or communication that do not use the word "signal" do not fire it. In the plot summaries it peaks on every "signal": the radio signal from the monolith, the Bat-Signal, a blocked bomb signal, a control signal, a signal device.

1659747.title: Assorted specific tokens, led by 樺
1659747.explanation: This first-layer unit reacts to the identity of the marked token itself, and the tokens do not share one meaning. The strongest is the Chinese/Japanese character «樺» (birch) inside names such as 樺山資紀, 樺美智子, 林樺慶 and 小白樺商店, followed by the source tag «新华网» (Xinhua Net) at the end of Chinese news items, the character «副» (vice, deputy), «力», the dash in "FILE PHOTO -", and word-ending fragments such as «atica» (Aquatica, Carnatica), «etro» (Meetro), «eman» and Russian «вая». In the plot summaries it fires weakly on the whole word «Batman» wherever it appears, regardless of the scene. There is no single idea here beyond a fixed list of unrelated tokens; the surrounding text does not matter.

1788084.title: Capitalised name or title right after "the"
1788084.explanation: The unit fires on a capitalised name or title that directly follows the word "the" and is used as a label for a person, family or revered thing: "the Wright brothers", "the Wright family", "the Dharma", "the Savior", "the Parson", "the Fuhrer", "the Shroud", "the Savage family", and more weakly "the Riddler", "the Joker", "the Waynes", "the Marquis". It reacts to the marked token itself (often the last piece of the word) in that "the + Name" slot, not to the surrounding story, and the set of words is a loose handful (Wright, Dharma, Savior strongest) rather than one topic. The same names without "the" in front, or ordinary lower-case nouns after "the", do not appear among its firings.

1799394.title: "Luthor" name piece; split comic-character names
1799394.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the piece "uthor" that completes the surname in "Lex L-uthor" (also "President Luthor" and a bare "Luthor"), in comics articles and Superman or Justice League plots, whatever Luthor is doing in the sentence. At about two-thirds strength it fires on the closing piece of other comic-book character names that are split into pieces: "girl" in Batgirl, "isher" in Punisher, "lett" in Howlett, "anna" in Zatanna, "am" in Shazam. The peaks never fall on the whole-word names standing next to them (Batman, Superman, Joker, Robin, Lois Lane), so it is the name-completing fragment of a recognised superhero-comics name that matters, not the scene or villainy in general.

1817787.title: Side characters' names in superhero comics text
1817787.explanation: Fires inside text about comic-book superheroes (DC and Marvel articles, film plots, cast and member lists) at the point where a named supporting character or villain is mentioned, on the name or a piece of it. Harley (Quinn) is by far the most regular trigger and accounts for every one of the plot-summary hits; Shredder, Tomar-Re, Nimrod, Nebulon, Ursa, Agatha Harkness, Bianca, Paras and Obadiah show the same thing. The tokens differ every time, so it is the comics setting plus a secondary character's name that matters, not a spelling; the lead heroes' own names (Batman, Superman) never sit at the peak. A few strong passages do not fit the name pattern (" Naval", " magazine", a letterer's first name " Cory") although they are still in comics articles, so part of the signal is simply the comics context.

1826947.title: Superhero first names in comic-book text
1826947.explanation: The unit fires on the name token itself: an ordinary first name or name-piece that belongs to a comic-book hero, read inside text about superhero comics, films or games. The core set is the Fantastic Four and their neighbours (Johnny, Sue/Susan, Reed, Torch, Silver, Sub-Mariner, Triton) together with Billy (Batson), Barry (Allen) and Spy (Smasher). It fires on these names even when they belong to someone else in such a text (Johnny Viti, actor Johnny Duncan, actress Susan Misner, Susan Johnson, voice actress Kimberly Brooks), and more weakly on other names there (Nora, Panessa, White House). It does not fire on Batman villain names such as Dent, Penguin or Riddler, which belong to the opposite pole.

1834957.title: Names of superhero team members, mainly X-Men
1834957.explanation: The unit fires on the name of a member of a superhero team or a hero's ally when the text is about comic-book superheroes. The strongest cases are X-Men members: Iceman (peak on 'eman'), Nightcrawler and his real name Kurt, Magik, Phoenix, and Warren and LeBeau (the real names of Angel and Gambit); more weakly it fires on Batman's allies Dick Grayson and Oracle. It reacts to the name token itself in a comics setting, so the same first names also fire it for comics writers and artists (Kurt Busiek, Kurt Schaffenberger, Warren Ellis, Salvador Larroca), for Kurtwood Smith in a Green Lantern cast list and for a mobster called LeBeau in a Hulk film. It does not fire on the lead heroes or the villains of the same texts (Wolverine, Xavier, Magneto, Batman, the Joker), nor on Superman's Kryptonian names, which belong to the opposite pole.

1847046.title: Tampering with or erasing records, data, memories
1847046.explanation: The unit fires on the word, or word piece, that names an act of covertly interfering with information: tampering ("tam" in tamper, Chinese 篡改), erasing (erase, erased, erasing, erases: files, criminal records, memories) and illicitly taking or listening (Chinese 竊聽 eavesdrop, 竊取 steal). It reacts to the marked word itself, in English and in Chinese alike, and the surrounding text is usually about hacking, spying, records or memory wipes. Weaker firings are looser relatives: plans being "altered", "mind control", "hack into", and once Japanese 閲覧 (browsing the net). Text that only mentions computers, files or memories without such an act of altering, wiping or stealing does not fire it.

1849652.title: The "X" of X-Men; "Cop" of RoboCop
1849652.explanation: It reacts to a particular token inside a franchise name: most strongly the " X" that begins "X-Men" or "X-Force" (after "the", "Uncanny", "Avengers &" and so on, in Marvel comics text, and once on the Chinese for "Professor X"), and equally the "Cop" in "RoboCop". A weaker, related group in the plot summaries is the name of a comic-book group, substance or thing with a coined label: the gang "the Mutants" (on "ants"/"ant"), the "Venom" drug, Wayne "Enterprises", the aircraft "the Bat". It is driven by the name token itself rather than by the scene, and it does not fire on the personal names of individual characters from the same stories (Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver, Maximoff belong to the opposite pole).

1851670.title: Names of recurring supporting characters in crime series
1851670.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when it is the name of a familiar secondary character in a police-procedural or DC-comics setting: McGee in NCIS episode summaries (the strongest cases), Detective Kevin Ryan in Castle, Barbara Gordon, Clark Kent, Dick Grayson, and the town of Smallville, usually as the character is listed among teammates, allies or relatives. A second, weaker group is criminal-justice role words in the same kind of text: probation (officer, helper, sentence), ADA, and a prosecutor's first name (Reid). It does not fire on the lead characters named in the same sentences (Gibbs, Tony, Ziva, Batman, Castle, Beckett), and a few peaks (costumed, non-edged) do not fit either group.

1854180.title: Specific name tokens: Alfred, Barrett, Gambit, Scarecrow
1854180.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself, not to the scene: it fires on a small set of particular name pieces. The main groups are the name Alfred (Batman's butler Alfred Pennyworth, in plots and cast lists alike), the second piece of Barrett/Barret ("ret", "rett" after "Bar", for any person of that name), the "it" that completes Gambit (the X-Men character) and the "crow" of Scarecrow; a weaker, unrelated group is a few Chinese words such as 剛剛, 剛才 and 等等. What is happening in the story does not matter (Alfred fires whether he is beaten, dying or merely listed), and other character names in the same passages do not fire, so this is a handful of memorised spellings rather than one idea.

1857437.title: Secondary character names in superhero comics text
1857437.explanation: The unit fires on a capitalised name or codename of a secondary character, team or place inside text about superhero comics and their screen versions (Marvel, DC, Arrowverse, Heroes): Echo, Roy Harper, the Royal Family, Dwarf Star, Destroyer, Voodoo, Limbo, Yukio, Hiro, Doctor Arthur Light, and in the plot summaries Hurt, Jezebel and Maxie Zeus. Many of these are ordinary words or common first names used as a name, and 'Arthur' and 'Echo' recur even outside comics (King Arthur, Arthur Bach, Arthur Fleck, Echo Park), so the unit is partly tied to those particular words. It does not peak on the lead hero's own name (Batman, Tony Stark, Clint Barton) or on ordinary uses of the same words. A weaker, loosely related group is names and titles in Three Kingdoms history articles (Hanzhong, Marquis), plus one stray identifier in Java code (Macros).

1860920.title: Fragment inside a split word or compound name
1860920.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when that token is one piece of a longer word or compound that has been split into pieces, not to what the text means. The strongest cases are the Japanese character 差 opening compound verbs (差し引く 'deduct', 差し押さえる 'seize', 差し置く 'pass over') and other word-internal pieces in Japanese, Korean, Greek and Spanish (積雪, 積み, 기획, 콩쿨, rehabilit-ación, ἀποκαρτερῶν). In English it fires more weakly on pieces of names and hyphenated compounds: Rec-ode, Shoe-ing, horseshoe-arch, Milwaukee Braves, Bat-man, Bat-Signal. The topics are unrelated (tax law, roads, baseball, temples), so this is a loose spelling-level pattern rather than one idea, and ordinary whole words in running text do not fire.

1861692.title: Urban planning and land-use terms
1861692.explanation: Fires on words from town planning and land development: "greenbelts" / "green belts", "land" in developer or planning-body names (Urban Land Conservancy, Urban Land Institute, World Class Land), "vacant lot" / "vacant land", the planner Robert Moses, and now and then an architecture or street-layout word (metabolism, sinuous, straightened). It depends on the surrounding text being about how a city, neighbourhood or site is laid out, zoned or redeveloped. Housing-product words such as condominium, condo and amenity belong to the opposite pole. In the plot summaries it is weak and loose, landing on place-like terms (Batcave, the Narrows) and on the name Arthur.

1861897.title: Tail piece of a compound label before its noun
1861897.explanation: No single clean idea; the unit reacts to the marked token itself, which is nearly always the closing piece of a compound or derived describing word inside a noun phrase that is still going. One group is suffix pieces that finish an unusual adjective or name before a noun (ectoplasm-ic residue, Teut-onic lesbian, leather-mask-ed thugs, Boot-y-licious, fluor-opol-ymers, IE-C); a second group is the second noun of a label for a kind of group or venue (ball-room culture, rave-style club scene, vampire club, Evil Organization, Space Criminal Organization, representation system, and la-ir in the superhero summaries). The passages lean toward drag/LGBT nightlife pages and villain groups in Japanese superhero plots, but the same words standing alone as a plain head noun, or ordinary one-piece adjectives, do not show up. The weaker firings on 'Bruce' (in 'Bruce Wayne') and 'team-ing' are only loosely related.

1867375.title: Inner word-piece of a rare or foreign name
1867375.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a fragment in the middle or at the end of an unusual word that the tokenizer has split into pieces, most often a rare surname or place name (Bell-u, Bar-ad-ee, Pied-mont, Hou-mer, I-acon-o, Ma-ama, Ben-al-oh, De-ven-ish) and also pieces of Armenian, Korean and Chinese words or an odd code identifier (wipe-PS, set-osa). The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter; the passages range from biographies and military history to code and fight records. Common names and ordinary whole words that are a single token do not fire it, and in the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on similar split or unusual words (Uph-am, work-ah-olic, Osc-orp, lighten, Halloween). The pattern is loose rather than tied to one spelling.

1869035.title: Thing-noun completing a fictional place or gadget name
1869035.explanation: Fires on the token that completes a capitalised proper name of a place, building, vehicle, device or work title in a fictional world, where that last part is an ordinary thing-word or its ending: Bat-Signal, utility belt, Arkham Manor, the Raft, Helicarrier, the Garden / Magic Garden / Meteor Garden / Enchanted Garden, Ebony Tower, Golden Lance, The Burrow, Elsinore, Water Curtain Cave, GCPD. It reacts to the marked token as the closing piece of such a name, mostly in superhero, fantasy and myth material, and the Bat-Signal is by far the strongest case in the plot summaries. It does not fire on names of characters built from common words (Man in Black, Tin Man, Hatter go to the opposite pole), nor on the same nouns used as plain common nouns.

1871585.title: Closing piece of a compound term or name
1871585.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when that token finishes a multi-piece fixed term or proper name, so that the whole term has just become recognisable. It is strongest in Chinese encyclopedia text: the character 積/积 in 沉積(岩) 'sedimentary (rock)' in geology articles, 书/書 closing a Bible book title such as 玛拉基书 or 腓利門書, and similar term endings (質量數, 星周盤, 棘下筋, 프로야구). In English it fires more weakly on the last piece of a name (Dominey, Bathsheba, Mrs. Cod) and, in the plot summaries, on 'City' in 'Gotham City' near the start of a summary. There is no single meaning behind it: the topics range from geology to the Bible to character names, and the opposite pole of the same neuron also fires on name endings, so ordinary whole words and many other name endings do not trigger it.

1880565.title: Label noun stuck directly onto a name or number
1880565.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a plain noun that says what kind of thing, or what relation, the item just named is, when it is attached straight onto a name, a bracketed actor name or year, a number or a one-letter symbol with no comma, "of" or "'s" in between. Two related groups: kin and role words after a person's name ("Sarah (Kiara Advani) daughter of", "(born 1976) mother of three", "Jyoti (Resham Tipnis) husband", "Paramahamsa (Prithvi) guest house"), and category or measure words after a number or symbol ("Book 2 Chapter 14", "series 1 episode", "643 runs", "magnitude 7.6 star", "T parameter", "v value", "(1986) novel", "unit vectors", "density matrix" after a missing formula). In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on the possessive "'s" or a group noun right after a name ("Park family", "Nakatomi Corporation", "Grady sisters", "Falcone's"). It does not fire on the linking word "of" after a symbol or term, which is what the opposite pole takes.

1886436.title: The brand name "DC" / "DC Universe" (comics)
1886436.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: "DC" used as the comics publisher and franchise brand (DC Comics, DC Database, DCU Guide, DC Rebirth, DC Animated Universe, DCEU), and most strongly the word "Universe" coming straight after "DC" (the DC Universe setting or the DC Universe streaming service that carried Titans). It fires wherever that brand label appears, in article openings, section headings, external-link lines and category lists alike. In the Batman summaries it fires on the same "DC" tokens and, more weakly, on Batman-specific words such as Batcomputer, Batcave and Bruce. Other entertainment brands and rival-publisher characters (Showtime, Marvel's Human Torch or Vulture) do not fire it; they drive the opposite pole.

1910798.title: Famous leader's name recurring in historical narrative
1910798.explanation: Fires on the bare name of a famous ruler, commander or statesman (Napoleon, Andrew Jackson, Alexander, Cortés, Gandhi) when a history or biography text mentions him again as the one acting, typically at the start of a sentence or clause or after a title such as "President" or "Emperor". The peak is on the name token itself, but it depends on the earlier text having set up that figure and a historical account of war, government or conquest. It fires much more weakly on other central named actors that recur in a story (Nixon, Batman, Facebook, the GAA), and names in Arabic-style name chains (Abu Muhammad, Abu Yusuf) belong to the opposite pole.

1916049.title: Closing piece of a multi-part name or set term
1916049.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when that token finishes a name or fixed term that spans more than one piece. One group is the last fragment of an unusual or foreign word or surname that the model splits up: the "a" of Aga / Agaev (four of the top passages), the "el" of kugel, the end of Huttner, Tannen, Schmidlapp and an Arabic name. The other group is the second word that completes a set compound or title: AIDS crisis, Climate crisis, AIDS Healthcare, breast care, Image caption, Medical Encyclopedia, Typhoon-class, Arkham City, and the Chinese word for a rail line. It does not fire on the first piece of such a name or on ordinary free-standing words, and the groups are only loosely one idea.

1936244.title: Completing DC Comics names: Siegel, Finger, Jason Todd
1936244.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a well-known proper name from the DC Comics world, once the comics context and the first part of the name have been read: creators (Jerry Sie-gel, Bill Finger, Mort Weising-er, Joe Sh-uster), characters (Jason Todd above all, also Barbara Gordon) and titles (Detective Comics, Crisis on Infinite Earths, Golden Age). In the plot summaries it is almost entirely the "Todd" of Jason Todd, the second Robin, with a weaker hit on "Detective Comics". It reacts to the recognised name being finished, not to the scene: other names in the same passages (Bob Kane, Billy Batson, Tim Drake, Dick Grayson) do not peak, and ordinary surnames or the word "comics" outside this DC setting do not set it off.

1939271.title: Closing piece of a split-up proper name
1939271.explanation: The unit reacts to the token itself: a word-internal fragment that finishes an uncommon proper name the tokenizer has broken into pieces, such as the «o» of Donnie Darko, «bar» of Dunbar, «ir» of Altamirano, «enberg» of Blankenberghe, «ridge» of Dandridge, «ton» of Paxton, «ali» of Mahankali and «ès» of Dantès. The names are surnames, place names and film titles in any language or script (English, German, Spanish, Arabic text with Latin titles, Hindi), and the first fragment very often begins with D or contains a + n/m/k (Dark-, Dun-, Dand-, Dant-, Dag-, Blank-, Adam-, Altam-). The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter, and it does not fire on whole-word names or on ordinary words that are split; it is strongest where the fragment makes a recognisable name complete.

1952331.title: No single idea: surnames and struggle words
1952331.explanation: I could not find one idea. The strongest passages fall into two loose groups: the last word of a person's or thing's name, usually a short surname that is also a common word (A. D. Hope, Ted Ross, George H. R. Ross, Sam Ross, Mack Hall, Dwight-Lloyd, Three Dog Night, Wade, Carmichael), and a word that completes a phrase about struggling, declining or holding on (overcome, struggling upward, give up hope, begins losing weight, survive the ordeal, starts doubting her sanity, road to senility, vows, falling out). The link between the two groups is unclear (the word "hope" appears in both), the activations in the plot summaries are weak, and the unit seems to react to the marked token rather than to a scene.

1967232.title: Token that completes a recognisable fixed name
1967232.explanation: Fires on the token that locks in a specific multi-part name or compound belonging to some specialised world: Elite«XC», Cobble«pot», Afro-Cub«an», Blue Waho«os», World Artistic «Gym»nastics, Mr. «Olympia», Land «of» Fire, Blüdh«aven», Bat-com«puter», Alphon«se», and «Alfred» or «Gordon» right after "butler" or "Commissioner". The subjects are unrelated (mixed martial arts promotions, minor-league baseball teams, gymnastics championships, dance styles, anime, Batman's cast and places), so what is shared is the form: the text has set up a branded, organisational or fictional name and this token confirms which one it is. Surnames of ordinary real people do not fire it, and there is no single meaning behind the firings.

1980491.title: Phrase specifying which "one" is meant
1980491.explanation: The unit fires where a sentence singles out one particular member of a kind of thing already mentioned and begins to say which one: on the stand-in word "one" ("such as the one in London", "nothing like the one shown on the menu", "similar to the one that heads to Spain") or on the small word that opens the identifying detail after the noun, usually "in", "at" or "with" ("the one in Corias", "like the one at Anthony's Nose", "like that in our own State", "another hansom with the lean chap", "a candle with its wick dipped", "In one there was"). The weaker firings are looser versions of the same thing, a word that starts a describing phrase attached to a noun ("a safe containing", "a tesseract made up of", "a rose on his body", "in one ... and in the other"). The same prepositions used for plain place or time, with no noun being picked out or compared with another of its kind, do not show up among the examples.

1991492.title: Later word-piece completing an uncommon proper name
1991492.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a second or later sub-word piece that finishes or continues an unusual proper name that the tokenizer has split, at the moment the name becomes recognisable (El-gin, Barr-on, Nunci-ature, Garas-iev, D'M-ello, Diou-f, Keny-atta, Truck-ee, Gandhid-ham, F-ries, Cro-c, Ice-berg). The names are surnames, place names, institutions and nicknames from any subject (wrestling, cast lists, Vatican diplomacy, horse pedigrees, railways), so the topic does not matter; often the name or a related form has already appeared earlier in the text. Common words, and names written as one ordinary token, do not fire it, apart from a few weaker cases such as the whole word 'Oswald' or 'Scrolls' inside a title. The opposite pole fires on a similar kind of name piece, so what separates the two poles is not clear from these passages.

2004467.title: Surnames of well-known fictional franchise characters
2004467.explanation: The unit fires on the family-name token of a famous fictional character from a TV series, anime, comic or film franchise, usually right after the given name and often on the last piece of the surname (Chuck Bart-owski, Lucy Heart-fil-ia, Gregor Cleg-ane, Naruto Uzum-aki, Kakashi Hata-ke, Kate Aust-en, Peeta Mell-ark, Ollie/Thea Queen). It reacts to the marked token itself as the recognisable surname of a character it knows, and more weakly to such a surname used alone or in an estate or company name (Wayne Manor, Wayne Enterprises, Quinzel, Stark). It does not fire on given names, on nicknames in quotation marks, or on the names of real people such as wrestlers and musicians, which belong to the opposite pole.

2045342.title: Later piece of a spelled-out proper name
2045342.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a later sub-word piece of a proper name that the model has to assemble from several pieces, at the point where the name becomes recognisable (Kle-bold, Hear-st, Aeth-eling, Hag-ood, Crand-all, Le-efe, Diotre-ph-es, Butter-cup, Wink-lev-oss, El-ster, Az-rael). It is strongest for the surname of a real, often notorious or historical person given with the full name just before it (Dylan Klebold, Lee Harvey Oswald, William Randolph Hearst, Edgar the Aetheling), and weaker for fictional characters and odd spellings such as SPEEDWELL or TEOTWAWKI. It does not fire on the first piece of a name, on ordinary words, or on common names that are a single familiar token; the link is the spelling position inside a name, not the topic of the passage.

2063681.title: End of a scene-setting lead-in near a text's start
2063681.explanation: Fires in the first sentences of a summary, article or review, at the small word or comma that closes a framing lead-in and hands over to the actual content: "The opening scenes give", "The movie opens with", "against the backdrop of", "sets the stage", "In 1942,", "As he leaves for work one day,", "He observed that", a synopsis heading such as "Act 1" or the Chinese "story introduction". In the plot summaries it is weaker and lands mostly on the comma after an introductory clause ("Returning to his dorm,", "After receiving death threats,") or on the first main verb. It reacts to the position in the text (set-up finished, the story or statement about to begin) rather than to any particular word; the same commas and function words deep inside a story, away from an opening or set-up clause, do not fire it.

2065308.title: Victim noun right after a violent verb
2065308.explanation: The unit fires on the noun that names who is on the receiving end of a physical attack, just after a verb of violence: "breaks a guard's neck", "devours three sailors", "kills a cameraman", "stab a security guard", "fatally shoots several agents", "murders two guards". The targets are almost always unnamed people labelled by their role or side (guards, sailors, agents, henchmen, invaders, enemies, police, a protester), sometimes an animal (a coyote) or a group's property (the FBI helicopters, the police car). It reacts to the meaning of the preceding text (someone has just been killed, stabbed, shot or attacked) and marks the object of that attack; it does not fire on the attacker, on the violent verb itself, or on the same role nouns when they are the ones sent or ordered to attack (that is the opposite pole).

2071506.title: No clear idea; word-completing tokens
2071506.explanation: I could not find one idea. The peaks are scattered tokens that finish a word or phrase already begun: inner or final pieces of unusual names and long words ("ome" in Dahomey three times, "iron" in Doiron, "oux" in Guilloux, "zer" in Gozer, "ary" in cautionary, "lude" in prelude, "ation" in detonation, "pass" in Anpassungen), and abstract nouns that close a possessive or modified phrase ("his Nazi allegiance", "its original mandate", "his exercise", "his ability", "green plan", "la confrontation"). The subject matter ranges from war films to highway routes, botany and baseball in several languages, so the firing seems tied to the form of the token rather than to meaning, and even that description is loose and does not predict where it will not fire.

2079195.title: Names of a hero's famous supporting characters
2079195.explanation: It fires on the token that makes a well-known fictional proper name recognisable, most strongly the familiar colleague, assistant or love interest in a hero's world: "Lois" (Lane, many times), "April" (O'Neil), Pepper "Potts", "Moneypenny", "Lucius" (Fox), Dick "Hallorann". A looser second group is the completing piece of other pop-culture names and titles: "Brotherhood" in Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (three times), Apple "Bloom", "Netherfield", "Tenshinhan", Roxana, "GCPD", and a few plain name or title completions ("Hatcher", District "Deputy"). The unit reacts to the marked name piece itself in context; it does not fire on the hero's own name (Superman, Clark, Stark, Bond, Batman) or on ordinary words around these names.

2090182.title: Last piece of a suburb or district name
2090182.explanation: It fires on the token that completes a multi-part name of a local place, usually a suburb, neighbourhood or district inside or beside a larger city: North Shore (Auckland), North End (Boston), Newtown (Sydney), North Liberty, Burnsville, Pine Island, Northland, Miramar, and Chinese district names such as 庆安 and 番禺. The typical shape is a direction or plain word followed by a generic ending (Shore, End, town, land, Island, -sville), and the unit reacts to the ending once the name is recognisable, in geography, transport and local-history text. It does not fire on the first word of the name, on the big city or country itself (Auckland, Sydney, New Zealand), or on every compound place name. In the plot summaries it fires weakly on the closing piece of other compound names of places and characters (Batcave, Southern Isles, Killer Croc, Kingpin).

2109850.title: End of a name introduced with 'the'
2109850.explanation: Fires at the moment a name-like noun introduced by 'the' has just been completed: on the last piece of the name or, more often, on the very next word or mark (is, was, has, also, and, for, to, 's, a full stop, a closing quote). The nouns are proper names, titles, foreign words or coined labels that carry an article here: the Malini, the Lalla, the Loulia, the Ipomedon, the Wynn, the ARKA, the JI, The Inflore, the Balado's, the Batman's, the 'sunken place'. It is strongest of all when the noun after 'the' is missing altogether, as in maths text whose symbols were stripped out ('the imaginary part of the ,' and 'The  is called'). Ordinary 'the' plus a common noun, and names used without an article, do not appear among its firings.

2122779.title: Last piece of an uncommon multi-token proper name
2122779.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a proper name which the model has to spell out in several pieces: mostly people's surnames (Spann, Schanberg, Goudreau, Garibay, Axente, DeAnda, Milbank, Frei, the Chinese names 伍仲衡 and 劉慧卿, the wrestler Microman), and also places and invented names (Parzán, King County, Kings County, Gozer, Arkham). It reacts to the marked token itself as the closing piece of the name, in any language, both at first mention and when the name comes back later in the text. It does not fire on the first piece of the name, on common names that are a single token (Peter, Bruce, Dana), or on ordinary words; one Portuguese hit (the verb "assinar") is an exception.

2161966.title: Famous leader's assassination, death or top office
2161966.explanation: The unit fires on the word that names a defining late-life or peak-career milestone of a well-known figure, most often a head of state: the assassination of Lincoln, Gandhi or Kennedy, Stalin's death, Yuan Shikai proclaiming himself emperor, Obama's second term, or the top office itself (Prime Minister, Commander-in-Chief, former CEO, "later years of his life"). The peak sits on the milestone word (assassination, assassinated, death, term, Minister, Chief, CEO, life) and depends on the famous person named just before it; these phrases usually serve as a time marker ("after Stalin's death", "when Lincoln is assassinated"). It is strongest for assassinations of political leaders and only weak in ordinary plot summaries, where deaths of unknown or minor characters and early-career stages of a person's life do not trigger it.

2178472.title: Joint inside a terse description of someone
2178472.explanation: Fires part-way through a compact descriptive phrase that is characterising a person or thing, at the point where one descriptor has just been given and another is about to be attached. The peak is usually the joining token itself: "and", "who", a comma or semicolon, "of", "between" ("Hotaru's schoolmate and", "A fox-eared demon who", "former diplomat and", "Black body;", Hindi and Japanese equivalents of "and"), or the last noun of the descriptor ("robotic machines", "silicate mineral", "vigilante", "beauty queen"). It is strongest in character-list entries and dictionary-style definitions that open with a bare noun phrase, and weaker in ordinary plot sentences; the same connecting words in running narrative that is telling events rather than describing an entity do not set it off. The opposite pole, by contrast, sits on joints inside a term being named or defined ("dissolution of", "the idea that").

2251772.title: Plural noun endings closing an expected phrase
2251772.explanation: There is no single topic here; the passages range over code comments, Japanese, Korean, German, encyclopedia text and film plots. The loose pattern is about the marked token itself: it is most often the last piece of a plural noun that completes an expected phrase in the middle of an explanatory sentence ("phon-emes", "deced-ents", "martial arts", "change your clothes", "Official Olympic Reports", "1972 paintings", German "Lehrplä-ne", Korean plural marker "들은", "metahum-ans", "job offers"). The remaining cases are other highly predictable continuations of a phrase already under way ("external or internal", "all over the world", "the corresponding", "codifications of", "twenty years cannot"), so the fit is partial and the unit should be treated as only weakly understood. It does not depend on what the text is about.

2277703.title: Linking word before a stated origin or method
2277703.explanation: The unit fires in explanatory prose at the point where a sentence is about to say where something comes from or how it is obtained: its source, basis, cause, derivation or method. The peak sits on the small linking word that opens that statement ("developed based", "come straightforwardly from", "can be calculated as", "was influenced", "originated from", "in direct proportion to", "determined graphically", "engineered using"), and it also fires on name-origin sentences and on "Road/Route to the final" headings. What the text before it means matters more than the token itself: the same words "from", "as", "to" or "using" in ordinary narration of events fire weakly or not at all, and terse formal definitions ("is", "given by" before a formula) belong to the opposite pole.

2296861.title: Set-up clause finished, outcome or details due next
2296861.explanation: Fires at a joint in a sentence where a set-up has just been given and the text must now say what came of it or spell it out. The clearest case is the comma that closes an opening participle clause before the main clause: 'Impressed with MacKay,', 'Befriending Shruti,', 'Rightly interpreted and followed,', 'Misunderstood and carelessly handled,', 'Noticing Andy's increased commitment to the job,'. A second group is a statement that promises specifics to come: 'works as follows', Chinese '具体情况如下', 'does not go as planned', 'How is the State to acquire them?', 'Something certainly seemed to be the matter with Splash.' Weaker firings fall on small linking words just before a phrase of manner or result ('in style with', 'escape under', 'praising Remy without', 'alive and'); the unit follows the position in the sentence, not a topic or one particular word, and the three groups are only loosely one idea.

2298898.title: Word opening the content of a request
2298898.explanation: Fires on the small linking word that comes straight after a verb of asking, requesting, begging, demanding or calling out, at the point where the thing asked for is about to be stated: "requests «that»", "begs «for»", "petitioned «to»", "asked for his name «to» be removed", "cries out «for»", "insisted he «be»", "ask her to send «him»". It reacts to the meaning of the text before the marked token (someone is making a request, plea or summons) rather than to the word itself, since "that", "for", "to" and "be" all serve equally. Weaker firings cover going to look for or fetch something ("looking «for» bear", "to «retrieve»"); one passage ("According to the prophecy«,»") does not fit. It does not fire on advice to seek something ("advised to seek help"), which belongs to the opposite pole, nor on "that" or "for" in ordinary uses without a request.

2306707.title: Text set in the Star Wars universe
2306707.explanation: The unit fires when the text so far is about Star Wars: the galaxy, Jedi, the Empire and the rebels, Tatooine, Obi-Wan, Vader, the Death Star, in English, Chinese, Russian or Portuguese alike. The marked token itself does not matter; the peaks fall on ordinary words and word pieces (the, by, to, 's, shop, race, Ghost, voice, a comma, parts of names such as AAT, Krayt, Trandoshan, Tatooine) once the Star Wars setting is established. Weaker firings appear in other franchise plot summaries (The Land Before Time, an X-Men character, Man of Steel, The Lion King, Batman openings), so it leans loosely toward fictional-universe plot text, but the same function words in ordinary non-Star-Wars text do not fire it strongly.

2321679.title: Opening quote mark after a reporting phrase
2321679.explanation: The unit fires on the opening quotation mark (double or single) that starts a short quoted phrase set inside a sentence, right after a frame that reports someone's words or label: "described the winner as", "labelled Sunderland as", "proclaims that", "adding that he was", "called him", "shouting the phrase", "saying,". It reacts to the moment where narration hands over to someone's exact words, before any of the quoted words have been read. Weaker firings are loosely related at best: a reported claim or label without quote marks ("knows nothing about it", "honoring Gacy as an asset", "you know,") and a few unrelated word endings ("fixed point", "irregularly placed", the "au" of the name Gusteau). Quote marks that open ordinary dialogue at the start of a line, or closing quote marks, do not appear among the strong cases.

2364747.title: Superhero conventions: first appearance, costume, powers
2364747.explanation: The unit fires when the text is clearly about a comic-book superhero or supervillain and reaches one of the stock facts of that genre. In encyclopedia entries it peaks on the publication formula right after the character is introduced as a DC or Marvel hero ("made his first appearance", "first appeared in", "debuted in", "appearing in American comic books"). In plot summaries it peaks where the hero puts on or debuts the costume, gains or tests superhuman abilities (flying, absorbing energy, enhanced senses), adopts an alias or keeps a secret identity. It reacts to the superhero meaning of what came before, not to the words themselves: "first appeared" or "costume" in a text about an ordinary person, actor or film does not show up here.

2372268.title: Infinitive hanging off a noun: "X to be done"
2372268.explanation: It fires at the opening of a non-finite verb phrase: on "to" as an infinitive marker, or on the light verb right after it ("be", "have", "come", "having"). The strongest cases are infinitives attached to a preceding noun, amount or object that say what is to be done with it or what it is for: "demands £55,000 to be paid", "DNA evidence to be compared", "titillation to be had", "a spoon to eat", "a dress for my friend to try on", "a fatherly hand to guide him", "recruit Jones to recover". A smaller group is set phrases with the same light verbs: "To be fair", "never come true", "come to fruition", "interested in having her back". It reacts to the grammar at the marked word, not to a topic; "to" as a plain preposition of direction, and the predicate type "is not to be spoken of / is of no consequence" (the opposite pole), do not fire it.

2375398.title: Threshold of a discovery or announced news
2375398.explanation: Fires at the hinge just before the content of a surprise is stated: the "that" or "find" in "discovers to his horror that", "wakes the next morning to find that", "only to find that", "is shocked to see that", and the colon, full stop or exclamation mark after a teaser such as "we have good news:", "only to get another shock:", "can rejoice." or "Exciting news!". What it reacts to is the preceding set-up (someone comes upon or is about to be told something unexpected, often with an emotion word like horror, shock, joy), with the revelation itself still to come; the marked token is only the connector. Plain reported speech ("says that", "a letter stating that") fires weakly, and after-the-fact outcome phrasing such as "it turned out" belongs to the opposite pole.

2396903.title: Superhero comic-book world: heroes, powers, Superman
2396903.explanation: The unit fires when the text is clearly set in the world of superhero comics (Marvel, DC and similar). It is strongest on the word "in" of the stock encyclopedia opening "is a superhero / supervillain appearing in American comic books", on "powers" when heroes use their powers to save or fight, and on the name Superman or things tied to him ("Superman foe", "enemy of the Justice Society", LexCorp, metahumans). It reacts to the superhero setting built up by the preceding words rather than to one particular token, so the peak token varies. It does not fire on the "Powers and abilities" lists of skills and healing (that is the opposite pole), nor on ordinary film plots without costumed heroes.

2474730.title: Era and wartime references in superhero-comics text
2474730.explanation: Fires in writing about comic-book superheroes (Marvel and DC character articles, Captain America plots) at the moment the text places something in a historical period: 'World War II' (on 'II' or 'War'), a 1940s year (on the '4' of 1943, 1941, 1947), 'during the' Golden or Silver Age, 'the '70s'. The marked tokens differ, so it reacts to the context before them, a superhero text reaching a wartime or period reference, and not to one particular word. In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on the background description of a hero: 'peak of human' perfection, 'secret government agents' after Pearl Harbor, years of training, a photo from World War I. The word 'super' itself (superhero, superpowers) belongs to the opposite pole, and a few peaks (Birds of Prey, 'first public Ultras', War Machine, World's Finest) are comic-book names with no era in them, so the pattern is not perfectly clean.

2483435.title: Last word of an invented place name
2483435.explanation: Fires on the ordinary noun that completes a made-up, capitalised name of a place, institution or object inside a fictional world, mostly comic-book, superhero and fantasy settings: Star «City», Central «City», Savage «City», Arkham As«ylum», Black«gate», Wayne «Enterprises», Hell's «Kitchen», Stone «Table», Bone Eater's «Well», Future Gadget «Lab», Ivy «University», Turtle «Van», Atomic Cauld«ron», New New «York». The unit reacts at the point where the generic word (city, asylum, lab, table, well, van) closes the coined name, often inside quotation marks; it is not tied to one word. It does not fire on the first word of such names, on the same nouns used as plain common nouns outside a name, or on character aliases such as "the Shadow".

2495485.title: "Man" as generic type or mankind
2495485.explanation: The unit fires on the token "man" (or the "'s" right after it) when it stands for people in general or a type of person rather than one individual: "man's best friend", "every man for himself", "everyman", "the white man", "white man's graveyard", "Black Man's Kryptonite", "the average man", "man-made", "man's most terrible weapon", German "des kleinen Mannes". Set phrases and sayings with generic or racial-category "man" are strongest. It fires only weakly when "man" is a part of a compound such as "manhunt", "one-man" or "Man-Bat", or refers to a particular man ("a missing man").

2500843.title: School or place word inside a proper name
2500843.explanation: The unit fires on a generic institution or place word in the middle of a capitalised proper name or title, above all 'High' and 'School' in named schools and titles: Degrassi Junior High, Sweet Valley Junior High, Riverside High School, Tides High School, Eastside High, Lakeridge High School, and High School Musical (peak on 'School'). Weaker firings follow the same shape with other words: Grand Hotel Chiambretti, North Britain, X-Men: Evolution, Grandview U.S.A., and in the plot summaries 'Gotham' when it heads a name such as Gotham City Bank, Gotham City Police Department, Gotham Cemetery or Gotham clock tower. It reacts to the marked word as part of a name that is still being spelled out; the same words in ordinary lower-case use ('high school outcast Eddie' in one passage) are not where it peaks.

2524311.title: Someone's judgment or emotional reaction toward another
2524311.explanation: Fires when the text reports how someone regards, judges or reacts to a person or event: opinions and criticisms 'passed on' someone, gossip, a belief or expectation, or a feeling such as surprise, dismay, admiration, disgust, fear, respect or astonishment. The peak falls on the word that names the attitude or ties it to its target ('judgments passed on', 'with dismay', 'admiring', 'fears', 'expecting', 'believes', 'condemns', 'Impressed', 'Convinced,'), and the same thing happens in Hindi, Japanese and Korean, so it reacts to the meaning of the preceding text rather than to a particular token. Plain narration of actions and events with no onlooker's opinion or feeling does not fire it. The pattern is fairly loose: a few strong passages (a character repeating a remark, someone receiving a piece of news) are only loosely about a stance.

2525198.title: Return to the text's central famous figure
2525198.explanation: Fires when the text names again (or says 'he' for) the one person or entity the whole passage is about, usually as the subject of a new clause right after an opening time or situation phrase: 'After the victory at Granicus, Alexander', 'In February 2015, Trump', 'The film jumps forward to 1996. Jobs', 'throughout the 1990s, Apple', 'earlier that day, he'. It is strongest for famous real figures who are the topic of a biography or history (Lincoln, Alexander the Great, Leonardo, Newton, Jobs, Trump, Achilles), also for a company or country that is the topic (Apple, Turkey), and more weakly for the hero of a story (Batman, Holmes, Peter).
