It reacts to who the name refers to, not to the spelling, since 'he' and the Chinese name for Alexander also fire; side characters and other names in the same passages (Philip, Darius, Greeley, Sculley, Watson) do not.

2548640.title: Start of the verb after a character's name
2548640.explanation: Fires on the token that comes straight after the short name of a person already introduced in a story or history, usually the first piece of the verb saying what that person now does, often to someone else: Li «mut»inied, Valkenheiser «pun»ishes, Sun «over»threw, Dobrynya «over»comes, Ko «happens», have Ge «stripped», Chill «test»ifies, Batman «sub»dues, Zero «fle»es, Lucy «be»friends. A looser group is the small linking word after a name that is being acted on (introduced George «to», sends Jean «to», Tesla «while», Tetsu«,») and, in code, the symbol right after a short variable name (u«+»1, L«mc»). It is a loose positional pattern rather than a topic: the single strongest case (a mutiny) stands well above the rest, and the peaks do not share one meaning or one word.

2550644.title: Superhero comics lore: eras, dates, numbered Earths
2550644.explanation: The unit fires when the text before the peak is about American superhero comics and their history, almost always DC Comics (Golden Age heroes, Wonder Woman, Robin/Nightwing, the 1960s Batman TV series, the multiverse). Within that setting it peaks on small tokens that place something in the lore: "Age" in "Golden Age", "mult" in "multiverse", a digit inside a publication year or decade (1941, 1960s), the number of a parallel Earth (Earth-2, Earth 11), or words like "the", "campy", "Two", "Robin", "sidekick", "first" in "the first Robin". It is the comics subject that drives it, not the token: the same years, digits and "Age" in ordinary history or film text do not appear, though two weaker-fitting cases (a digit in "20th century" in a Wonder Woman creator biopic, and "26 dimensions" in an Arabic physics article) show it also leans a little on digits in general.

2562846.title: Falling short or overdoing: reproachable omission or excess
2562846.explanation: The unit fires where the text says that something that should have happened did not, or that something was done beyond the proper measure: "failing to save", "did not respect the agreement", "did not write", "failed to achieve orbit", "name missing", "nearly misses", "communication cut off", and "too many", "too much", "overstate", "overgeneral". It reacts to the meaning built up before the marked token (a failure, omission or excess measured against what was expected), and peaks on the small word that carries it (not, to, too, over, save, missing), very often inside a grievance, rebuke or criticism ("for not saving him", "rebukes Scottie for not doing more", "she at least might have sympathized"). It does not fire on plain harm, danger or disaster with no sense of a missed duty or exceeded limit; those (crash, injuries, risk, toxic) belong to the opposite pole.

2584477.title: Henry VI, Mozart, Bruce: identifying names and digits
2584477.explanation: It fires on the token that pins down which specific, well-known person or number is meant, in factual encyclopedic text. The passages fall into three loosely related groups: the regnal numeral after 'Emperor Henry' (VI, VII, and the Chinese 亨利 of 亨利四世); the name Mozart, usually when it recurs as the subject of a music article; and the last distinguishing digit of a year or serial number (1777, 1778, 196 BC, 223 BC, UFC 234, a verse range 2:3-6), often one already given earlier in the document. In the plot summaries it peaks on 'Bruce' each time the text turns to Bruce Wayne, and not on 'Batman', 'Joker' or the other names in the same sentences. It reacts to the marked token itself rather than to a scene or idea, and the groups do not reduce to one clear concept.

2612008.title: Comic character profile: start of powers/biography section
2612008.explanation: Fires inside encyclopedia-style entries about comic-book heroes and villains, at the moment a new section opens and the text is about to describe the character: on the heading "Powers and abilities" and the first words after it ("X has", "X possesses", "X is"), and on the first token of the character's name right after a "Fictional character biography" sub-heading. It reacts to the situation (a superhero profile about to state what the character can do or who he is), not to one word; the same words "abilities" or "has" in ordinary prose do not trigger it. In plot summaries it fires more weakly where a hero's skills are being listed ("trained to the peak of human physical perfection and an expert in martial arts", "uses his technological inventions") and on rosters of named villains.

2622633.title: Home organizing and decor; wrestling and character rosters
2622633.explanation: No single trigger word: the peaks land on many different tokens (organizing, organize, cabinetry, pattern, spout, a comma, 'the', 'women', 'Bank', 'Queens', 'Five', 'lawful'), so the unit reacts to the topic of the text before it. Two loose groups share the top passages. The first is household how-to and home-style writing: organizing kitchen cabinets or a garage, decluttering and minimalism, arranging plants and plant stands, installing a faucet, patterned fabrics, handbags and luxury home finishes. The second is popular-entertainment text that describes a cast or roster of performers and characters: women's wrestling tag teams, factions and valets, a TV series title, a role-playing character class, a villains list and, weakly, plot summaries that introduce an ensemble cast, a sidekick or gang members. Ordinary narrative of plot events and unrelated technical or news text do not fire it; the link between the two groups is not clear.

2625356.title: First word after a deleted item in text
2625356.explanation: The unit fires on the token that comes right after a hole in the text, where a measurement, number, name or title has been stripped out and the sentence carries on without it: "a [missing length] gravel runway", "a [missing size] indoor and outdoor shopping complex", "a [missing area] ballroom", "used by [missing name] trains", "[missing number] masculinos y femeninas", a Russian "In 1906 [missing name] achieved", and Chinese empty brackets, empty title quotes or a comma straight after a dropped name. It is reacting to the gap before the marked token (often a double space or an ungrammatical join such as "a indoor"), not to the marked word itself, which varies freely across languages. The same words in intact sentences do not trigger it, and it barely fires in the plot summaries, where nothing has been removed (the weak hits there show no pattern).

2625481.title: Continuing a reference to a famous figure
2625481.explanation: The unit fires on a small word or word-piece that carries on a reference to a well-known named figure, story or tradition that the text has just invoked; the marked token varies widely ("the", "that", "his", "it", "and", "as", "family", "Manor") and is not the trigger by itself. Two groups stand out: religion and sacred story (the tale of Rama and "the" Hindus, being a Buddhist and what "that" meant, Adam "and" Eve, the atonement of Jesus Christ, Moses and the Apostles, Gandhi) and famous characters or pop-culture names (James Bond and "the" part, Doraemon and "his" friends, the Beatles and "It", and in the plot summaries the Joker as "the" character, the Wayne "family", Wayne "Manor", his dual "identity"). A few strong passages (DPLL solvers, parabola, the IPCC as a body) do not fit either group, and similar function words after dry institutional or legal subjects do not fire, so this is a loose pattern.

2629416.title: Superhero comics: heroes versus costumed villains
2629416.explanation: The unit fires when the text before the marked token is clearly inside superhero comic-book fiction, and most of all when it is talking about a hero's enemies: it peaks inside words such as "rogues" (rogues gallery), "supervillain", "super-heroes", "vigilante", "Injustice Gang" and "villains", and on plain words like "the", "to", "of" or "battle" in sentences where a costumed hero fights, chases or spares a named villain. It is reacting to the meaning of the passage (the superhero-and-supervillain genre and its character biographies), not to one spelling, so the peak token varies a lot. Ordinary crime, war or action stories without costumed heroes and villains do not fire it; a masked-wrestler persona is a weak, loosely related case.

2648630.title: Completing word of a famous brand name
2648630.explanation: The unit fires on the word that completes a very well-known, fixed, capitalised name of a franchise, event or institution: above all "Wars" in "Star Wars", then "Bowl" in "Super Bowl", "Bank" in "Money in the Bank", "free" in "Get out of jail free", "Affairs" in "Veterans Affairs", "Sentai" in "Super Sentai" and the "0" of "G20". It reacts to the marked token as the moment the stock name is recognised, not to the surrounding topic, which ranges over actor biographies, wrestling, news and film plots. In the plot summaries it is much weaker and fires on the franchise-branded "Bat" of "Batmobile" and "Bat-Signal", on "Batman #500", and on "the" just before "history of Batman comics" or "Joker". Ordinary two-word phrases that are not a famous set name do not trigger it.

2649804.title: Real personal names, especially heroes' civilian names
2649804.explanation: The unit fires on a token of a specific person's proper, real-world name, usually part-way through the name: a given name whose surname is about to follow (Bruce, Barbara, Victor, Clifford, Barry, Oliver, Connor) or the surname just after it (Gordon, Palmer, Grayson, Wayne, Howard, Powlett). The largest group is the civilian or secret-identity name of a comic-book character (Bruce Wayne, Barbara Gordon, Victor Fries, Ray Palmer, Barry Allen); a second group is formal names in catalogue-like text: peers (Harry Powlett, Thomas Howard), a Chinese surname (Sima), and the Latin genus of a species name (Vermivora, Carcharhinus). It does not fire on costumed code names such as Batman, Green Arrow, Firefly or Hawkeye, which belong to the opposite pole.

2650301.title: Mid-way through familiar names: Alzheimer's, Sesame, Bruce
2650301.explanation: No single clean idea. The most common trigger is the word Alzheimer (in "Alzheimer's disease", "Alzheimer's patients", a tag "alzheimers") and nearby medical terms ("monoclonal antibody", "presenile dementia"); a second group is foreign versions of Sesame Street (Plaza Sésamo, Bonjour Sésame, Sesamstraat); a third is fast-food franchising (franchisee of Burger King, master franchise of McDonald's). What these share with the weaker plot hits (Bruce before Wayne, vigil before -ante, Anglo-A before -fghan, La Ni before -ña, February 14) is that the unit fires part-way through a well-known fixed name or term, at a point where the rest is highly predictable. It does not fire on the completed name or on ordinary words in the same passages, and a few peaks ("the", a list number, a year digit) fit none of this.

2655879.title: Start of a repeated or expected item
2655879.explanation: Fires on the first token of an item whose content is already fixed by the text before it. One group is a name, term or identifier being restated from earlier: 'KSAFA' under a KSAFA heading, 'Informatics' after 'Faculty of Informatics', 'Engels' in Latin letters after his Chinese name, lower-case 'amar' and 'copic' after the capitalised names, 'r.message' inside Message(), 'clientBuilder' reusing the parameter, 'self.CONSTRAINT' inside constrain(). The other group is the next entry in a running series: 'Dec.' in a month-by-month list of attacks, '13 July 1909', '1911:' under a 1911 heading, 'long.' after 'lat.', the first name of a player list, the first 'return' of a function body. It reacts to position and predictability, not to any one word, so a name, date or identifier appearing for the first time in ordinary prose does not fire it; the pattern is loose and a few passages ('Welti moves', the Chinese '試圖') fit only weakly.

2663170.title: End of a place name locating something
2663170.explanation: Fires as a named place is completed or on the word right after it: the last word of the name ("New Zealand", "Islamic Republic of Pakistan", "king of England", "Downtown Baltimore", "Gotham City") or the plain noun or preposition that follows a place used as a label ("Bel Air schools", "Delaware shore", "Stratford road", "Brighton & Hove league", "Harvard University", "New York in", "Ivory Coast in", "Cincinnati for", "Alsek since"). The text before it is naming a country, state, city, river or region to say where something is or which place it belongs to. In the plot summaries it extends to a named fictional setting or franchise followed by its generic noun ("Gotham City", "the Lego universe", "Batman comics"). The same nouns (schools, road, league, city) without a proper place name before them do not fire it.

2667574.title: Clause joint in old-fashioned argumentative prose
2667574.explanation: The unit fires inside long, reasoned sentences of essay-like or sermon-like writing (mostly 19th-century books on rhetoric, religion, science, law and invention), at the joint where one part of an argument has just been laid down and its counterpart or consequence is due. The peak is a comma, semicolon, full stop, exclamation mark or a small linking word (and, by, would, should, are, it, to), typically after a rhetorical question opening ("Why should", "Can my invention be made to do better work by", "must it continue undecided,"), a concession ("bien que non identifiée,", "but it"), or the first half of a balanced pair ("the other would", "the learned by the more learned;", "call it X or name it Y,"). It is not tied to any one word and does not respond the same way to the same punctuation in plain storytelling: plot summaries fire weakly, the strongest being "themselves are killed by an" and "forgives her and", which share only the mid-sentence hinge position.

2670458.title: Subject-area word inside a title or label
2670458.explanation: The unit fires on a word that names the subject area or kind of a thing in the middle of a noun phrase, usually a modifier just before the head noun or the object of "of/to/on the": "University Art Show", "guide to a Horse", "Notes on the Ornithology", "the Motorcycle Rental Landscape", "Shiny R", "Inestabilidades Solares", "the NFL record", "the environmental footprint", "the Earth's mantle", "South African provincial tournament", "privacy and security". The strongest cases sit in catalogue-like text: lists of awards, schools, courses, episodes, buildings, bibliographies and police blotters, in English and Spanish. In the plot summaries it is weak and lands on the same kind of classifying word ("college football team", "War Department", "black market", "crime scenes", "sheepdog trials", "beauty pageant"). The pattern is loose: it is the role of the word as a topic or category label, not any one word or theme, and plain narrative nouns that do not classify a following noun do not trigger it.

2697085.title: Index digits and placeholder slots in code
2697085.explanation: The unit fires almost only in source code, on a token that merely fills a positional slot: a small index number inside brackets, parentheses or format braces (arguments[1], args[0], matcher.group(3), {0}, {2}, #1), or a throwaway single-letter variable that follows an earlier one in a declaration or loop (var n ... var b; for i, j; var r, e; the y in (x z (y z))). A smaller related group is dummy or blanked-out filler standing where real content would go: '*****', '* * *', the test value 'pippo', and empty brackets. Meaningful identifiers, ordinary numbers in prose and normal narrative text do not trigger it; in the plot summaries it is essentially silent (at most 0.12 of its maximum).

2708627.title: Inside a fixed multi-word name or model designation
2708627.explanation: The unit fires partway through an established multi-word label that names a specific thing, at the point where the rest of the name or the noun it labels is predictable. The strongest cases are car articles: "previous generation" / "second generation" / "first generation" just before the model name, and chassis or version codes such as E30, S130, R32 and Mk1. A second group is set phrases and proper names in other fields ("inverse square root" algorithm, the "Choi" matrix, "War on" Drugs, "Press F to" pay respects, "Steve Rogers", and in plot summaries "Gotham" City, "Clone" Wars, "Griffith" Observatory, "Hell's Kitchen"). It does not fire on ordinary descriptive words or on free, non-fixed noun phrases; the plot-summary firings are much weaker than the car-generation ones.

2724250.title: Inside a proper name after a definite article
2724250.explanation: Fires partway through, or just after, a proper name that is introduced by a definite article (the, le, la, l', du, des, Portuguese a): place names, titles of works, and titled characters such as "the Côtes-d'Armor", "du Mont-Dore", "du Torchon brûle", "l'Ascension du Haut-Mal", "the Havre-Saint-Pierre region", "the Shredder", "the Joker", "the Ten Rings". The peak usually sits on the first piece of the name, when the rest is predictable (often because the name already appeared earlier in the text), or on the word right after it ("The Ile-de-France has", "the Okanagan was"). It is strongest for French and other non-English names in encyclopedic text; names without an article and ordinary common nouns after "the" do not show up, and the pattern is loose rather than tied to one word.

2751771.title: No clear pattern; detail-ending tokens deep in long texts
2751771.explanation: I could not find one idea. The peaks fall on unrelated tokens: the last piece of a place or personal name (Monte "Carlo", East End "Park", Patrick "Tam", Luc"iani", Mah"oney", Back"us"), the last digit of a sports score (34-3"1", 45-1"3"), ordinary nouns closing a phrase (continental "countries", African "coast", Omnib"uses", anth"ologist"), the first piece of an uncommon word ("spur" track, "pl"iers, "wig"wams), and a colon inside a code error string. The only loose common thread is that the strongest firings come far into long, dense or list-like documents (film lists, credit lists, exhibition lists, bowl-game results, old books) on a token that finishes or nearly finishes a concrete detail; in the short plot summaries it barely fires (at most 0.36) and on scattered words ("past", "prisoners", "birthday", a comma), so it does not track any story content.

2783773.title: A device or mechanism being triggered or operated
2783773.explanation: The unit fires where the text describes a piece of machinery or a rigged device doing its job or being set going, peaking on the word that names the action or function: detonate, explode, set off, rigged to (explode), a bomb, self-destruction, and also lift (mechanism), revolving (light), reeling (machine), garage door (opens/closes), lighting (control), airlock, and 'activates the' or 'lever connected to the' just before the system is named. The two groups are bombs and explosives being triggered (the bulk of the film plots) and ordinary mechanical or electrical apparatus named by its working function (bridge lift, lighthouse lamp, sonar reel, gas-lighting, the Chinese 'vasomotor' centre). It is not a general violence or explosion detector: shootings, fights and deaths without a device being actuated do not appear, and the strength is modest outside mechanism-type wording.

2799181.title: Mixed: generic stand-ins, blank slots, structural marks
2799181.explanation: No single idea covers the strongest passages: the peaks fall on " ter" in "terroir", an empty gap where a place name or number was stripped out ("The line from [blank] was", "- [blank] 85 scholarships"), a masked "*****" in code, a table bar, a dash, a bracket, and the pronouns "it" and "he". The only loose thread, clearest in the weaker passages and in the plot summaries, is a plain low-content word that stands in for a specific thing already set up earlier instead of naming it: "the city", "her own country", "his war-ravaged country", "their party", "the President's". That thread does not explain the top six passages, and the plot-summary firings are weak (under 0.3), so this unit should be treated as not understood.

2830013.title: Looming harm or threat that forces a reaction
2830013.explanation: It fires in narrative and history when the text has just stated a threat, a danger or a bad turn of events that is about to push someone to act, give in or change course: a feud that has gone too far, a daughter wasting away, a threat to burn the fort to the ground or to blind a husband, realizing a bad mistake, anticipating that a case cannot be won, a rival who may follow suit, someone's existence being jeopardized, bombs about to be detonated. The peak token itself varies (far, away, damage, that, suit, ground, threatened, to, this, a comma or full stop), so the unit is reacting to the meaning of the clause, not to a word; the next clause usually gives the response (they agree, surrender, issue orders, hatch a plan). Plain reports of a death or a fight with no sense of pressure or impending consequence, and ordinary plot narration, do not set it off.

2853400.title: Superhero or comic-book hero being named
2853400.explanation: Fires when the text is naming or describing a costumed comic-book superhero: on the word "superhero", "hero" or "character" in phrases like "a fictional comic book character" or "a monkey superhero", and on hero names such as Superman and Supergirl (often mid-name, on "man", "erg", "Super"). It also fires, more weakly, where a plot lists superpowers, a made-up hero identity or a costume ("the costumed vigilante", "Kosmoboy", "Bat Lady"). It reacts to the superhero meaning of the context rather than to one spelling, so ordinary heroes, characters or people in non-comic stories do not trigger it; a few of the plot-summary hits ("along", "rad" in a 1943 serial) do not fit and look like loose pulp-adventure spillover.

2880987.title: Re-mention of something named earlier in the text
2880987.explanation: The unit fires in the middle of a running story or description at the moment the text points back to a person or thing that was already introduced earlier in the same document: a repeated name (often on a token inside the name, as in Aakash, Eterno, Diabolus, Mariella, Vadivelan, Marguerite, Fleming) or 'the' plus an earlier noun (the car, the vault, the local officer, the fiancee, the Ark, the captain, Charley's house, earlier that day). It also fires when a list or a line of code repeats items given before (a dead cat, a pile of bottles; the cake, not father; a function signature written a second time). It reacts to what the earlier text set up and what is being picked up again, not to any particular word, and it does not fire on a first introduction of a new character or object. The pattern is loose: the peak tokens themselves are varied and some passages fit only weakly.

2950589.title: "a/an" after has/had: introducing an attribute
2950589.explanation: It fires on the indefinite article "a" or "an" that comes straight after a verb of having or including (has, had, have, with, includes, features, grants him), at the point where a description is about to name a property the subject possesses: "has a population", "has an average elevation", "had a capacity of 70,000", "had an important historical role", "has a new young girlfriend", "features a large ensemble". It is strongest in encyclopedia-style sentences about towns, places and characters. It reacts to the article itself in that position: when the having verb is followed directly by an adjective, a plural or another verb ("has won", "possesses characteristics", "featuring sleek design") it does not fire, and "a" in other positions is not what drives it.

2957052.title: Two people acting or bonding as a pair
2957052.explanation: The unit fires when the text has just brought two (occasionally three) named parties together and now treats them as one joint unit doing something mutual: becoming friends or lovers, agreeing on something, sharing a secret, talking privately, or setting off together. The peak falls on the small word that carries the togetherness, such as "them" in "sees them together", "their" in "their relationship", "they", "we" in "the matter we discussed" and "the date we agreed", "and" in "and the two became friends", "together", "between", "agree" or the start of "elopement". It responds to the meaning of what came before (a pair has formed or reached an understanding), not to the pronoun alone: a plain "they" or "their" for a crowd, or for people who are not acting jointly, does not produce it.

2979147.title: Text about superhero comics and their heroes
2979147.explanation: The unit reacts to the subject of the surrounding text, not to one word: it fires inside articles and summaries about superhero comic books and their characters (DC, Marvel, Dark Horse titles, costumed crime-fighters, people with superpowers). Within such text the peak lands either on words of that vocabulary ("superhero", "heroes", "super"power, "Comics", "don" a costume, "people" with superpowers, resuming vigilantism) or on the digits and spaces of publication dates and issue numbers in a comic's publication history. Dates, cast lists and the word "hero" in texts that are not about superhero comics do not set it off; one loose case is the film about the creator of Wonder Woman, where it fires on a year just before the comic enters the story.

3005424.title: Just before naming a famous story's companion character
3005424.explanation: Fires on the comma, preposition, role word or name fragment that comes immediately before a well-known character of a famous fictional universe is named, so it is anticipating the next word rather than reacting to the marked token: 'Princess Leia, [Lando]', 'their nephew, [Luke Skywalker]', 'his first officer, [Spock]', 'a reincarnation of [Pigsy]', 'despite [Sam's]', 'Bender as the [Tin Man]', 'Wayne's butler, [Alfred]', 'his ward, [Robin]'. The strongest cases are members of an iconic cast (Star Wars, Lord of the Rings, Journey to the West, Star Trek, Oz), and it works the same in Japanese, Chinese and Russian text; weaker cases are any point in a novel where a character name is due ('said [Braye]', 'close to [Frank]'). It does not fire on the name itself once written, and slots where a place or setting name is due ('the city of', 'set in') belong to the opposite pole.

3046518.title: Slot where a specific number or name follows
3046518.explanation: The unit fires at a point where an exact identifying detail is just beginning or about to be filled in, mostly in text about films, comics and other fiction. One group is numbers: the "#" or first digit of a comic issue or volume number ("vol. 2 #7", "Captain America #41", "Batman #484", "Earth-712"), a digit inside a year ("20|04"), or a count of years ("for twenty years", "after 6,000 years", "four thousand years before"). The other group is names: a role word, comma or bracket right before a character or actor name ("news reporter" Terri Morales, "psychiatrist" Hugo Strange, "three orphan girls," Margo..., "Mary Margaret (" Ginnifer Goodwin) or the first part of a name whose rest is still to come ("Dr. Ruth", "Leslie", "Grand P", "The Brave"). The marked tokens themselves have little in common, so it is about what comes next, not a word; the pattern is loose, and plain mentions of famous franchise names (the opposite pole) do not trigger it.

3051398.title: Character taking on a named alter ego
3051398.explanation: The clearest group is fiction where a person is tied to a costumed or second identity: Jack Napier before and as he becomes "the Joker", Jason Todd as the second Robin, a hostage adopted as the new Harley Quinn, Harry Osborn calling himself Green Goblin, the original Invisible Man, Jekyll and Hyde. It fires on the man's own name (Napier) or on the small word just before the persona's name is given ("the", an opening quote mark, "of", "new", "second", "original"), so it partly anticipates the alias. Two unrelated groups also appear: cancer-biology text about the tumour suppressor gene p53 (TP53, Mdm2-p53, retinoblastoma) and brackets in Java command-line parsing code. Ordinary mentions of heroes or villains with no origin, succession or renaming do not show up.

3053127.title: DC Comics titles, teams and issue numbers
3053127.explanation: Fires in text about the DC Comics universe at the start of, or inside, a DC-specific proper name: the first word of a series or team title ("Teen" Titans, "All" Star Comics, "Green" Lantern Corps, "Dark" Archer), the "#" or digits of an issue number after Detective Comics or National Comics, and character names ("Night"wing, "Ra"'s al Ghul, "Doctor" Destiny, Calendar Man's "Day"). It reacts to the DC setting established before the token and the name that is beginning, not to any one word. Comparable superhero text about Marvel and the X-Men drives the opposite pole instead, and the same words outside a DC context are not present.

3060980.title: Just before a predictable family name or surname
3060980.explanation: The unit fires on the token immediately before a surname or family name that the context has already made predictable, so it is reacting to what comes next rather than to the marked word. The marked token is either a first name or its last piece (Thomas [Wayne], Jack [Drake], Tim [Drake], Jason [Todd], Lysa [Arryn], Hanabi [Hyuga], Isabella Linton, Mina [Murray]) or a linking word that leads into a known name: "the" before Simpsons, Kents or Lees, "de" before Wolowitz, "and" or a comma between famous chess or tennis players, and the Chinese name-separator dot or "和" before Dursley, Simpson, Berners-Lee or Nadal. It needs a known fictional family or famous person whose name can be guessed; ordinary first names in rosters, genealogies and marriage records (John, James, Daniel, George followed by an unguessable surname) do not fire it and instead drive the opposite pole.

3084566.title: First piece of a compound term
3084566.explanation: Fires on the opening word or word-piece of a multi-part term whose remainder is predictable, before the piece that completes it: "content" (marketing, creation), "site" (map), "link" (building), "web" (pages), "system" (service layer, System-Technology), "Information" (Architecture), "associate" (professor), "source" (_dir), "Man" (-At-Arms, -Bat), "man" (hunt, or), "crime" (-fighting), "Head" (of), "Children's" (Mercy Hospital), "couldn" ('t). The strongest cases are business, marketing and technology jargon in assistant conversations and press releases; in the plot summaries it is the first half of hyphenated or split names and words. It reacts to the token being an unfinished first element, so the same words standing alone as complete nouns, or the second element of the compound, do not fire it. A few peaks ("a system of", "requesting help") fit only loosely.

3088216.title: Opening token of a new code line or name
3088216.explanation: The firings fall into two groups that share only a loose idea: the first token of something whose rest is still to come. In source code it fires on the token that opens a new line after earlier header material: a repeated `from` starting another import line, or a `#` starting a fresh comment right after a licence block or at the end of a file (also an opening docstring quote or the `<` before a URL). In prose it fires on the first word of a multi-word proper name or title, almost always a short, common first name or nickname word: Peter (Parker, David, Maximoff), Big (Bad Mama, Boy, Bill Dust), Jason, Johnny, Pete, Tim. It does not fire on the surname or later words of the name, on rare or unusual names, or on tokens in the middle of a code line.

3103387.title: Last syllable of a person's surname in East Asian text
3103387.explanation: It fires on the final piece of a person's name, usually a surname and usually a repeat mention, in Chinese, Japanese or Korean encyclopedia prose: Regan, Smuts (史末资), Gould (グールド), Noyori Ryoji (野依良治), Euclid (欧几里得), Marshall (마셜), Trotsky (트로츠키), Xi Jinping (習近平), Kekkonen (케코넨), Cahill, Kellner, Valens (발렌스), Horowitz, Urbain (위르뱅), López (洛佩斯), Müller. The name is typically about to be tied to something of that person's (their book, party, regime, successor, era, claim), and it may be written in local script or in Latin letters inside the CJK sentence. The reaction is to the name ending itself, not to the topic of the article, which ranges from wars to chemistry. In English plot summaries it is much weaker (under 0.4) and lands on surnames or name parts such as Fries, Yinsen, Miller and the "'s" of Ra's al Ghul; surnames in bibliography or name lists in European languages belong to the opposite pole and do not fire it.

3119045.title: Superhero-comics text: dates, credits, time openers
3119045.explanation: The unit depends on the topic being a comic-book superhero property (Batman and Gotham, DC Comics, Wonder Woman, Marvel, Nick Fury, Captain America), and inside such text it peaks on small linking tokens rather than on the names themselves. One group is real-world production and publication facts: the first digit of a year or a release date ("September 2013", "From 2015", "in 1972", "October 10"), and credit words such as "debuted by", "published by", "creator", "alongside", "Publisher –". A second group is plot summaries of the same heroes, on the comma after a time-setting opener ("In 1917,", "In the present,", "The following night,") or on a named figure being brought in (Falcone, "with" the Joker, Gordon's "wife"). Dates and credits in articles on other subjects do not appear, and in-universe lore about lesser DC heroes belongs to the opposite pole; the peak tokens are varied, so this is a topic context more than one sharp trigger.

3120546.title: Music article about to name song or label
3120546.explanation: The unit fires in writing about musicians (mostly electronic, hip-hop and indie acts) at the point where a specific song title, record label, release platform or collaborator is about to be named. Typical peaks are the opening quotation mark of a track title after an artist's possessive ("Kraftwerk's "", "LMFAO's "", "the song ""), the first piece of a label or platform name after "released on / through" (Bandcamp, Mixmash, Diplo's label), and "with" in "collaborated with" or "song" just before the title. It is driven by the music-release context plus the expectation of a proper name next, not by one word. Quotation marks, "with" or company names outside music writing do not trigger it; its firings in the film plot summaries are weak (under half strength) and unrelated.

3125600.title: Mid-description of buses, trams and transit fleets
3125600.explanation: It fires inside Wikipedia-style text about bus, tram and rail operators, part-way through a phrase that specifies a vehicle, just before the vehicle type, model name or number arrives: "eleven 35 foot [buses]", "40-foot [Euro-style buses]", "low-floor [double-deckers / buses / tram]", "Stagecoach Gold branded [Alexander Dennis Enviro400]", "Mercedes-Benz Citaro, [Mercedes-Benz Cito]", "longer [articulated buses]", "6-meter light buses to [18-meter]", "Line [41]", "nine [1,200-ton submarines]". What matters is the transport-fleet setting built up by the earlier text plus the position in the middle of a size, floor-type, brand or model description, not any one word; a few peaks fall on the first digit of a year in an operator's history ("December 2016", "In 1987", "In 2013"). In the plot summaries, with no transit content, it fires only weakly at a comma or linking word just before a name or specific detail ("dubbed" before Venom, "childhood friend" before Thomas Elliot, "exhibit at" before Gotham Zoo), so ordinary narrative does not drive it strongly.

3125944.title: Describing what an alcoholic drink contains
3125944.explanation: Fires inside text about alcoholic drinks (soju, cocktails, margaritas, wine, vodka, brandy, liqueurs) at the point where a drink is being described, compared or broken into its ingredients. The peak sits on small linking words or mid-phrase tokens ("made of", "bottle of", "and" triple sec, "more kick than", a comma in a list of spirits, "peach" schnapps), so it is driven by the drinks topic before the token, not by the token itself. Food descriptions without alcohol do not show up, and two strong passages about coinage and paper money do not fit; the plot-summary hits are weak and unrelated (names and job titles such as Arthur, warden, officer).

3126057.title: Linking word just before a specific name
3126057.explanation: Fires on a small connecting word or verb at the point where the text is about to supply a specific named member of an established cast or set, so it is reacting to what comes next rather than to the marked token: 'he [and] Shredder', 'while [facing] Killer Croc', 'hired [by] his arch-enemy Professor Zoom', 'taken [to] the Brotherhood's leader', '[dismantle] the Penguin's', 'board [member] John Daggett', 'exception [of] Harley Quinn', 'his [wife] Martha', '[fulfill] Ra's al Ghul's', 'Saved [by] a second Harley'. Most strong cases are plot or cast text from franchises with many named characters (Batman and other DC stories, Game of Thrones), often just before a villain or ally is named or the next entry of a roster or numbered list. A second, smaller group is text about encryption and file-security software, just before a specific technical term ('a different [key] exchange', 'MD5 as a [Key] derivation function', 'also [uses] CloudRAID', 'such [as]'). The same words 'and', 'by', 'to', 'of' in text where no particular named entity or term is due next do not fire it.

3130157.title: Slot where a named associate or firm is introduced
3130157.explanation: It fires at the point where a role or relationship label is about to be filled with a specific name, either on the token just before the name ("built by", "old friend", "his friends at", "pregnant wife", "his partner,", "corrupt assistant,", "trusted mechanic)", Chinese "由" before a contractor) or on the first name itself (FBI profiler Benton, Captain Howard, hitman Pierre, Roger the subcontractor, Loeb). The passages fall into two related groups: supporting characters in crime and investigation plots introduced by their role, and building or engineering articles naming the firm, contractor or professional body credited (UIA, RAIA, BS EN standards, "designed by", "built by"). It is driven by what is about to come next rather than by one word; a few weaker peaks ("drying or wetting", "notoriety when", "can visit", "chase", "pressure", "traced to") fit only loosely, and it does not fire on the main character's name or on a name given without a preceding role label.

3131221.title: Start of a famous film or franchise name
3131221.explanation: The unit fires at the opening of a name that belongs to a well-known film or fantasy franchise: the first token of a title ("The" Dark Knight, "The" Hobbit, "The" Godfather, "El" Senor de los Anillos, the first letter of the Russian and the middle of the Chinese title of The Lord of the Rings, "Batman" Begins), the word just before such a title (Tarantino's 2007 "feature" Death Proof, 2009 "film" Inglourious Basterds), or the first piece of a coined franchise term (Hor-crux, Uruk-hai, Broomhilda, Bat-Signal, Batcave, Batsuit, Ra's al Ghul). It seems to mark the point where the model has recognised which famous work or franchise object is being named and the rest is predictable, with Tolkien, Batman, Harry Potter and Tarantino films the most frequent. It does not fire on the linking words "of", "or", "and" that lead into television series titles (the opposite pole), and the weaker firings on plain words such as "the", "his" and "real" are only loosely related.

3135718.title: Inside DC Comics / Watchmen comic-book lore
3135718.explanation: The unit reacts to the surrounding subject, not to the marked token: it fires inside encyclopedia-style text about DC Comics superheroes and villains, Watchmen and Alan Moore's comics, on small linking tokens (and, by, of, as, a comma, a year digit, the first piece of a name) at the point where a creator, a minor character or a team member is being named, as in "created by Andy Diggle and Jock", "the meeting held by Riddler", "Nite Owl II, Bubastis", "the Dove, Lobo". In the plot summaries it fires the same way on the names of minor comics figures (Black Glove, Harold, Penelope Young) and at the end of voice-cast lists. The same words in ordinary film plots or general prose do not fire it; two strong passages about philosophy (Sextus Empiricus in Portuguese, Julian Savulescu's "all-purpose means") do not fit and are unexplained.

3147565.title: Slot just before a person's name is introduced
3147565.explanation: The clearest group is anticipatory: the unit fires on the job word or link word that sits right before a character's name is given for the first time, as in 'by businessman [William Earle]', 'board member [John Daggett]', 'represented by [lawyer Donald Gennaro]', 'new CEO, [Miranda Tate]', 'engaged to [an architect, Peter Keating]', 'about to marry [Richard Aiken]', 'Indy and [Marcus]', 'Zeckendorf and [Benjamin Swig]', 'and King [Tut]'. A second, looser group is technical text where a specific value or label is about to be filled in: the space or digit at the start of a number ('; 1 Pa', 'a 3 position', '100 kPa', 'September 2013'), the abbreviation 'BLK' in a statistics key, a list comma, 'Resource' before 'Constructor'. The two groups share only the sense of a slot that the next token will fill with a specific item; it does not fire on names once they have been given or on job words that are not followed by a name.

3153462.title: Link word just before a name or foreign term
3153462.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking token (and, of, is, called, as, to, a comma or an opening bracket) at the moment the text is about to supply a specific proper name or a word in its original language: 'Tyre and [Sidon]', 'Baal Melkhart of [Tyre]', 'The Hebrew name for this region is [Tarshish]', 'which he called [quipus]', 'wine jar ([karas]', 'from Hebrew: [word]'. It is strongest in scholarly writing about Hebrew, Phoenician, biblical and other ancient or foreign subjects, where a transliterated term or the second of a well-known pair of place names comes next; in the plot summaries it is weaker and sits on a role word just before a person's name ('crime boss', 'Sister', 'nee', 'as' in a cast list). It reacts to what is coming rather than to the marked word itself, so the same linking words in ordinary prose with no name or gloss due next do not fire it, and the look-alike 'City of [London]' does not either.

3154013.title: Linking word before a named city location
3154013.explanation: The unit fires on a preposition or other linking word (in, to, of, near, toward, at, from, into, over, and, a colon) at the moment a specific place inside a city is about to be named, so it is anticipating what comes next rather than reacting to the word itself. In the reference corpus almost every strong case is set in New York City: "connected to" Manhattan, "borough of" The Bronx, "boathouse in" Central Park, "East River near" the 59th Street Bridge, "edge of" Spanish Harlem, "Precinct in" Bedford-Stuyvesant; in the plot summaries the same thing happens for Gotham and its places (Arkham Asylum, the Batcave, the city's islands) and for a few other cities. The same prepositions before something that is not a place, and the place names themselves, do not trigger it; one or two passages ("c." before a date, "could destroy") fit only loosely.

3154686.title: Linking words in statistical-model assumptions and before names
3154686.explanation: The pattern is loose and falls into two groups. The strongest and most numerous firings are in statistics and probability writing (econometrics, semiparametric regression, discrete choice, hierarchical models, SETAR, the Chinese restaurant process, sampling code), on small linking words in the middle of a statement of what a model assumes or how something is distributed: "assumed to be" independent, choices "are" assumed, an observation "is" determined, might be "randomly" associated, sits at "an" occupied table, "init".sample(). A weaker second group is biography and plot text, where it fires on a small connecting word just before a specific name or detail is given: teaming "with" Paige, ring "name", Epiphany, confined to "the" Cambridge Hospital, neighborhoods "of" Roxbury, New "England" Medical College, "In 2"002, revealing herself "as", led "by" the Joker, his wife"," Nora. What the two share is only a function word mid-clause right before the specifying content; it is not a single word, and statistical topic alone is not enough, since formulas and theorem statements in mathematical text do not show up here.

3161421.title: Slot just before a specific name or type
3161421.explanation: The unit fires on a small connecting token ("new", "=", a comma, a bracket, a colon, or a preposition such as "at", "by", "in", "under", "of") at the point where a specific name is about to be written; it reacts to what comes next, not to the marked token itself. There are two groups: in source code (mostly Java) the slot before a class or type name ("= new" JButton, "new" Values, ", " INDArray), and in prose, mainly artist biographies, the slot before the name of a venue, festival, organisation or title ("at" the College Art Association Conference, "Presented by" Art in General, "Crip Time," Stedelijk Museum, "Batman:" Arkham Knight, "under" Wayne Tower). The same words do not fire in ordinary running text where a common noun or verb follows, and the activations are flat across very different passages, so the pattern is loose rather than sharp.

3161575.title: Just before a comic-book character is named
3161575.explanation: The unit fires in superhero and comic-book text on the small linking token that comes right before the name of a costumed hero or, most often, a villain: "such as", "including", "and", a comma or dash in a roster, "by", "with", "of", "dubbing himself", "Spidey villains". It is reacting to what comes next, not to the marked word: the context (Marvel, DC, X-Men, a rogues gallery, a cast or toy list) makes an individual codename such as Wolverine, Joker, Bane, Doom or Killer Croc the predictable next word. The same linking words in ordinary text do not trigger it, and neither do places where a team or group name is about to follow ("the team", "fellow heroes", "the Bat Family"), which belong to the opposite pole.

3163742.title: Link word before a name in comics text
3163742.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking token (in, of, to, from, with, and, a closing bracket or an opening bracket) or on a verb such as pursue or capture, at the point where a specific proper name is about to follow, and most often in dense DC comics and Batman reference text: 'appears in' before Teen Titans #55, 'appeared in' before Action Comics #894, 'the end of' before Red Robin #11, list breaks between issue entries, and the slot before Red Hood, Poison Ivy, Two-Face, the Penguin or the Joker. A second, smaller group is historical and biographical prose, where it fires on the first fragment of an unusual name (Ca in Caesonia and Caesoninus, C in Cilician, N in Nereide, j in Dejter) or on a preposition before a named place (belonged to Goldcliff Priory). It is not tied to one word, and the same prepositions in plain narrative with no name-heavy, catalogue-like context do not fire it; the two groups are related only loosely, so this is a pattern of position rather than one clear topic.

3166532.title: Comic-book art credits and Daredevil-world names
3166532.explanation: The unit reacts to the surrounding subject, not to one word: it fires inside text about comic books and costumed heroes, on small tokens that sit in two related places. One group is credit lines for who drew or published a comic, at the point just before the person's or company's name ("illustrated by", "colored by", "and artist", "art by George", "line art", "colorist", "the publisher", "from Harvey Comics"). The other group is names and nicknames from Marvel street-level hero stories, above all Daredevil ("Daredevil", "Bullseye", "The Punisher", Jack "The Devil" Murdock, "Foggy", Elektra's plot). The same words ("by", "as", "the") outside comics do not fire it, and writer credits such as "written by" belong to the opposite pole.

3171832.title: Start of a predictable name or term
3171832.explanation: The unit fires on the token just before a specific, largely predictable continuation, not on a particular word of its own. Two loose groups stand out: the first letters of names of rivers, lakes and peoples of the Caucasus and steppe (" T" of Terek River, Terskol and Teletskoye lake, " Sc" of Scythians), and small words or prefixes in science text that lead into a term for something infinite or huge ("be" infinite dimensional, "an" infinity, "becomes" very large, "super"giant, super"fluid", hypothesis "do" continuo). Weaker firings are the same shape with landmarks and coined names ("the" Blackpool tower, "the" Golden Gate Bridge, "a" wormhole, "od"yssey, "Lego" universe). It is not a single clear idea, and it does not fire on "the" before a franchise name such as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, which belongs to the opposite pole.

3176308.title: Link word just before an expected proper name
3176308.explanation: It fires on the small word, punctuation mark or first name-part that sits right before a specific, predictable proper name: "in" before Stony Point or Libreville, "de" before Auckland, the Russian "and" before Tbilisi, "New" before Canaan and London, "Dublin" before Institute, the quote mark before Spectator, the full stop before the next periodical (Punch, Vanity Fair) in a list of press notices, and the comma inside a publisher's name (Longmans, Green, and Co.). In the plot summaries it fires the same way before Gotham names and offices: "Gotham"/"City" before Police Department or police lieutenant, "of", "in" and "with" before Batman, Gotham City, Harvey Dent and Commissioner Gordon, and "daughter" before Barbara. So it reacts to what is about to come (a known name of a place, institution, publication or person), not to the marked word itself; the same link words before ordinary nouns do not fire, and the names here are British, European, north-eastern American or Gotham ones rather than towns in Texas or Oklahoma.

3181213.title: Preposition before a setting-specific place name
3181213.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking word that introduces a location (in, at, to, from, of, near, beyond, on, or the "and"/comma inside a list of places) at the moment a place name is about to follow, so it is reacting to what comes next rather than to the word itself. The strongest cases come in two related groups: far-north geography ("south of Bluenose Lake", "238 km from Arctic Bay", Nunavut, Northwest Territories, Frobisher Bay, Rankin Inlet, Melville) and named places inside a fictional world ("In the Riverlands", "a road in Astapor", "At Harrenhal"; in the plot summaries "At the Batcave", "returns to the Batcave", "an assault on Arkham Asylum", "live at Wayne Manor"). A few weaker firings are plain "at/near" phrases about a time or an ordinary venue. The same prepositions before ordinary ports, cities and dates in ship or biography articles ("departed Portland", "in Freeport", "to Vladivostok") belong to the opposite pole, so the pattern is only moderately clean.

3184941.title: Opening fragment of a split word, or a preposition
3184941.explanation: No single meaning: the unit reacts to the form and position of the token, not to a topic. In the reference corpus it fires on the short first piece of a word that the tokenizer has broken up, nearly always beginning with "d" or "und": "und-etermined" (one boilerplate sentence, "The event featured an undetermined number of professional wrestling matches", repeated across many EMLL Anniversary Show articles and making up most of the top list), "d-oppelgänger", "D-endermonde", "d-arker", "Led-ger". In the plot summaries it instead fires on a preposition or linking word that leads into a place or event: "a fire at Blackgate Prison", "took him to the abandoned Arkham Asylum", "break into Arkham Asylum", "buried the Joker beneath the asylum", "eighteen months after", "outside of", "so that". The shared thread is only that the token opens something still to be completed (the rest of a word, or the noun phrase after a preposition); complete ordinary words and the wrestling or Arkham subject matter by themselves do not explain it.

3190476.title: Preposition before a named English estate or institution
3190476.explanation: The unit fires mostly on a small locating word ("at", also "of", "to", "near", "in") just before the name of an established house or institution is due, most strongly in writing about the English aristocracy and its country seats: "plantings at" Houghton Hall, "housed at" Houghton Hall, "raised at" Holkham Hall, "hangs at" Lamport Hall, "his stud at" Euston Hall, "as at" Hatfield, "dined at" the Duke's house. It is anticipating the proper name of the seat, and the surrounding talk of earls, dukes, baronets and Walpole is what makes it strong. A smaller second group is the names of Victorian statesmen themselves (the middle of "Disraeli", the comma before "Mr. Gladstone"), and one passage about engineered receptors does not fit. In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on "to", "at" or "in" before a named institution a person is sent to, such as Arkham Asylum, prison or the amusement park; ordinary prepositions before common nouns or actions do not fire it.

3215045.title: About to name a specific organization or member
3215045.explanation: The unit fires at the point where the text is just about to name, or has just begun to name, a particular organization, group, network, restaurant or team, or a person identified by their place in one. It peaks on the linking word before the name ('hired at' Prune, 'member of' Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad, 'mole in' his father's organization, 'organisations like' the VVB, 'heard about' this restaurant, 'Black Glove member' Le Bossu, 'wide receiver' Andrew Hawkins) or on the first letter of the name itself (F in Freenet, N in NCC, NRB and NORSAR, the character 國 opening 國軍 and 國民黨). It does not fire on the generic words in the middle of long institutional titles such as Research, Graduate or Information (the opposite pole), nor on the same prepositions when no named body or member follows. The pattern is loose: the sentences from the plot summaries are weak and only partly fit.

3241037.title: Lead-in word before a technology or equipment noun
3241037.explanation: The unit fires on the linking word or modifier that comes just before a piece of technology, weaponry or equipment is named, so it is anticipating what comes next rather than reacting to the marked token itself. Examples: Chinese "使用" before laser technology, the particle "的" before a secret weapon, a fictional weapon or nanomachines, "outfitted with" a cybernetic torso, "advanced" android or DNA microarray, "high-powered" radio signal, "invasive" surveillance network, "female" robots, "steal" equipment, "using" a drug agent. It is strongest in Chinese and Japanese articles about video games, military hardware and science fiction; a looser group fires on the same kind of modifier or list-comma slot before non-technical nouns ("underground" band, "full-length" spectacle, "Toronto-based" company, lists like environment, energy, language), so the idea is not fully clean. It does not fire on the device noun itself.
